cases.title: Bike shop squeezed by tariffs
cases.judge: owner of an independent bike shop
cases.situation: The owner (judge) of a 9-year-old bike shop imports most bikes and parts from suppliers in Taiwan and China. Sales were $780,000 last year with a 6% profit margin. Tariff changes in 2026 raised the shop's costs on some products by 10% to 25%, and the owner isn't sure which tariffs will last after the Supreme Court's February ruling. A big-box store nearby sells cheaper bikes. The owner is considering raising all prices by 15%.
tasks: How global trade and tariffs affect the shop's costs
How prices work as signals in this market
Factors affecting the shop's profit
The role of government in trade
Political factors that create risk for importers
questions: Should I just raise all my prices 15% to cover the tariffs?
What if the tariffs change again next year?
model: Open: 'Your shop has survived nine years because customers trust you. Let's protect your margin without driving them to the big-box store.'

Global trade (EC:016): a tariff is a tax on imports paid by the importer, so it hits the shop's costs first. The average effective U.S. tariff rate was about 6.7% in July 2026, but about 22.8% on goods from China (Penn Wharton Budget Model).

Government and politics (EC:008, EC:113): on Feb. 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs, but Section 232 and 301 tariffs remain and new ones replaced some. Trade policy is a political risk the owner can't control, only plan for.

Prices as signals (EC:006): customers buying a $3,000 e-bike care more about fit and service than a $150 difference; customers buying a $400 kids' bike compare prices with the big-box store. So prices should rise selectively.

Profit factors (EC:010): at a 6% margin, the shop keeps about $46,800 on $780,000 in sales. Raise prices 8% to 10% on high-end bikes and service, hold prices on entry-level bikes, and grow repairs, fittings and rentals, which have no tariff exposure and higher margins.
Supplier strategy: get quotes from suppliers in Vietnam or Taiwan (lower-tariff sources) and order earlier to avoid rush shipping.
Cash plan: keep two months of operating costs in reserve and ask the bank for a line of credit before costs rise further.
Visual: a table of product categories showing tariff exposure, price elasticity and the recommended price change.

Judge Q1: Not across the board. Your entry-level customers will walk to the big-box store, so we'd raise prices 8% to 10% on premium bikes and service, where customers value expertise, and hold the line on kids' and starter bikes. Growing repairs and fittings, which have no tariff cost, protects the margin too.

Judge Q2: That's why we don't bet on one outcome. A second supplier in a lower-tariff country, a cash reserve and smaller, more frequent orders let you adjust within a season. If tariffs drop, you'll have room to cut prices and win customers back from the big-box store.

cases.title: A second restaurant while rates rise
cases.role: commercial lenders at a community bank
cases.judge: owner of a popular Mexican restaurant
cases.situation: The owner (judge) of a profitable restaurant wants a $250,000 loan to open a second location across town. The first location earns about $1.1 million a year in sales with a 9% profit margin. The Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026, and the bank's prime rate is about 7%. The owner also wants to add a fourth cook at the current location to handle weekend crowds, though the kitchen has only one grill line.
tasks: How interest-rate changes affect the loan decision
Where the economy is in the business cycle
How consumer spending affects restaurant demand
The law of diminishing returns in the current kitchen
Factors that affect the second location's profit
questions: Should I wait for rates to come down before borrowing?
Why not just hire more cooks at my current place instead?
model: Open: 'Your first location's numbers are strong. Our job is to make sure the second one adds profit instead of risk.'

Interest rates (EC:084): with prime near 7%, a variable-rate loan could get more expensive if the Fed keeps raising. Recommend a fixed-rate SBA 7(a) loan so the payment is locked; a $250,000, 10-year loan at about 9% costs roughly $3,170 a month.

Business cycle (EC:018): real GDP grew 3.4% in Q3 2026 and unemployment is 4.1%, consistent with an expansion, but inflation at 3.7% and Fed hikes suggest a late-stage expansion. Expand, but with reserves.

Consumer spending (EC:081): restaurants depend on discretionary spending. Real consumer spending was nearly flat in September 2026 and the saving rate was 3.8%, so budget the new location's first year conservatively, at 70% of the current location's sales.
Diminishing returns (EC:023): with one grill line fixed, a fourth cook adds little output and gets in the way. The bottleneck is equipment, not people.

Profit (EC:010): new-location costs include rent, staff, equipment and marketing. Break-even analysis: if fixed costs are $40,000 a month and the contribution margin is 60%, the site needs about $66,700 a month in sales to break even.
Plan: fixed-rate loan, six months of operating costs in reserve, a second grill line at the current site financed separately, and quarterly reviews with the bank.
Visual: break-even chart for the new site and a line showing the loan payment as a share of projected cash flow.

Judge Q1: Nobody can time rates. If the new location can earn more than the loan costs, waiting means giving up that profit. We'd lock a fixed rate now so future hikes can't raise your payment, with no prepayment penalty, so you can refinance if rates fall.

Judge Q2: Because of diminishing returns. With one grill line, a fourth cook adds only a little output while costing a full wage. The fix at your current site is a second grill line, and real growth comes from the new location's added capacity.

cases.title: A family worried about rising prices
cases.judge: parent of two who is worried about inflation
cases.situation: A 42-year-old parent (judge) earns $88,000 a year and has $46,000 sitting in a checking account earning 0.01% because 'cash is safe.' Grocery and gas bills jumped this year, and the client heard on the news that inflation is high and the Fed is raising rates. The client also worries about job security after a friend was laid off, and asks whether the economy is heading into a recession.
tasks: How inflation affects the family's buying power
How interest-rate changes affect savers and borrowers
What GDP and unemployment say about the economy
Opportunity cost of keeping cash idle
A plan that protects against both inflation and job loss
questions: Is it safe to move my money out of checking if a recession might be coming?
Why is the Fed raising rates if prices are already hurting families?
model: Open with empathy: 'You're right that prices are up. The good news is that higher rates also mean your savings can finally earn real interest.'
Inflation (EC:083): prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026. At 0.01%, $46,000 loses about $1,700 of buying power a year.
Opportunity cost (EC:001): the real cost of 'safe' cash is the interest and buying power given up.

Interest rates (EC:084): the Fed's target is 3.75%-4.00%, so FDIC-insured high-yield savings accounts and short-term Treasury bills pay far more than checking. Keep it insured: under $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
Economy (EC:017, EC:082): real GDP grew 3.4% in Q3 2026 and unemployment is 4.1%, so there's no sign of recession yet, but we plan for one anyway.

Plan: keep one month of bills in checking; move six months of expenses (about $27,000) to a high-yield savings account as the emergency fund; put $10,000 in a 6-12 month CD or Treasury bill ladder; invest the remaining $9,000 for long-term goals in a diversified index fund through a Roth IRA.
Budget: track grocery and gas spending, use store brands and price-matching apps to blunt inflation.
Visual: bar chart comparing what $46,000 is worth after one year in checking vs high-yield savings.

Judge Q1: Yes. A high-yield savings account at an FDIC-insured bank is just as safe as checking, up to $250,000, and it pays far more. In a recession, the emergency fund is exactly what protects you, so we keep six months of expenses there, insured and available any time.

Judge Q2: Because higher rates slow borrowing and spending, which brings inflation down over time. It feels painful now, but if inflation stayed at 3.7%, every paycheck would keep buying less. The upside for your family is that savers earn much more right now.

cases.title: A maple syrup company going global
cases.judge: founder of a family maple syrup company
cases.situation: The founder (judge) of a Vermont maple syrup company has $2.4 million in annual sales, almost all in the U.S. A distributor in Japan and a grocery chain in Germany want to carry the products. The founder has never exported, worries about getting paid, and noticed that the dollar has been strong, about 159 yen per dollar and well up against the euro since August 2026. The founder will travel to Tokyo next month to meet the distributor.
tasks: How exchange rates affect export sales
The global environment and ways to enter foreign markets
How trade alliances and agreements affect access
Cultural considerations for the Japan meeting
What the founder needs for international business travel
questions: How do I make sure the Japanese distributor actually pays me?
Should I wait for the dollar to weaken before I start exporting?
model: Open: 'Two international buyers asking for your product is a big opportunity. Let's make it safe and profitable.'
Global environment (EC:104): start with exporting through the distributor, the lowest-commitment entry mode, not opening an office abroad.

Exchange rates (EC:100): a strong dollar makes the syrup more expensive for Japanese and German buyers, and if the company bills in yen or euros, weaker currencies shrink the dollars it receives. Use forward contracts from the bank to lock in exchange rates on confirmed orders.

Trade alliances (EC:112): the EU is a single market of 27 countries, so the German chain can distribute across Europe once the products meet EU labeling rules. Check tariffs under any U.S.-Japan and U.S.-EU arrangements with the bank's trade desk.
Getting paid: a letter of credit guarantees payment once shipping documents are presented; export credit insurance from the Export-Import Bank covers buyer default.
Culture (EC:110): Japan is high-context; exchange business cards with both hands, expect decisions by consensus, build the relationship before price, and bring a small, high-quality gift.

Travel (EC:141): check travel.state.gov for Japan's entry rules, make sure the passport has enough remaining validity, enroll in STEP, buy travel medical insurance and use a card without foreign transaction fees.
Visual: a map with both markets plus a payment-flow diagram showing the letter of credit.

Judge Q1: Use a letter of credit for the first orders. The distributor's bank guarantees payment once you show the shipping documents, so you're not relying on trust alone. Export credit insurance from the Export-Import Bank adds a second layer. Once you have a track record, you can move to easier terms.

Judge Q2: No. Nobody can predict exchange rates, and these buyers want your product now. A strong dollar mostly matters for pricing, and we can manage it with forward contracts and a price that works for both sides. Waiting risks losing the distributor to a competitor.

cases.title: A credit union branch in an underserved town
cases.judge: CEO of a regional credit union
cases.situation: The CEO (judge) of a 40,000-member credit union is deciding whether to open a small branch in a nearby town of 12,000 people where the last bank branch closed two years ago. Residents now drive 25 minutes to bank or use check-cashing stores that charge high fees. Several small businesses there have asked for loans. The board worries the branch won't be profitable, since online banks are winning younger members with higher savings rates.
tasks: The role of business (and credit unions) in society
How small businesses affect the local economy
Competition from online banks and fintechs
The economic utilities a branch creates
The ethics of serving or not serving the community
questions: How can a branch in a small town ever be profitable?
Why not just tell those residents to use our mobile app?
model: Open: 'This town is an opportunity hiding in plain sight: thousands of people paying high fees because no one serves them.'
Role in society (EC:070): credit unions are member-owned cooperatives meant to serve their communities. Serving an underserved town fits the mission and builds loyalty.
Small business (EC:065): small businesses employ about 46% of U.S. workers (SBA, 2025). Loans to local owners create jobs and deposits.

Utilities (EC:004): a branch creates place utility (no 25-minute drive), time utility (Saturday hours) and information utility (financial education); possession utility comes from small-business and car loans.

Competition (EC:012): we can't win a rate war with online banks, so we compete on non-price factors: local lenders, in-person help and fast small-business decisions. Check-cashing stores are the real competitor here.
Plan: a small, low-cost branch (two staff plus an ATM and video banking) that pilots for 18 months with clear goals: 1,500 new members, $5 million in loans, break-even by month 18.
Ethics (EC:106): offer fair, transparent products, no surprise fees, and a free financial literacy class in partnership with the local high school.
Visual: a map showing the 25-minute drive and a projected break-even timeline.

Judge Q1: Keep costs low and target the business the big banks left behind. A small branch with two staff, an ATM and video banking costs a fraction of a full branch. Small-business loans, car loans and members switching from check-cashing fees can bring it to break-even in about 18 months, and we'd measure that every quarter.

Judge Q2: Many will use the app, and we'll help them set it up. But small-business owners and older members need in-person help for loans and bigger decisions. A small branch with video banking gives them both, which online banks can't.

cases.title: A regional bank versus fintech
cases.judge: president of a 90-year-old regional bank
cases.situation: The president (judge) of a regional bank with 60 branches has watched customers under 35 move their paychecks to fintech apps and online banks. Deposits from that age group fell 12% in two years. The bank still earns most of its profit from the spread between loan and deposit rates. Its decision making is slow: a new app feature needs approval from five layers of management. The president asks how the bank should respond.
tasks: Different business models in banking
How organizations adapt to today's markets
Competition in financial services
Factors in the business environment
How the bank's organizational design slows it down
questions: Should we just copy what the fintech apps do?
Won't closing branches drive away our loyal older customers?
model: Open: 'Your bank has something fintechs don't: 90 years of trust. The goal is to pair that with the speed customers now expect.'

Business models (EC:138): the bank earns the interest spread; many fintechs, such as Chime, earn mostly interchange fees from debit card swipes (Chime S-1, 2025). Different models mean the bank shouldn't copy blindly.
Environment (EC:105): technological (mobile, AI), social (younger customers expect instant service) and economic (higher rates make deposits more valuable to compete for) factors all matter.

Adapting (EC:107): more customers manage accounts by app than by any other method (44% in ABA's Oct. 2026 survey; about 10% prefer branches). Priorities: early direct deposit, instant transfers, no-overdraft-fee options and a better app.
Competition (EC:012): compete on non-price strengths, such as local lending, advice and trust, while matching fintechs on basic convenience.
Organization (EC:103): five approval layers is a tall structure. Create a small, cross-functional digital team with authority to launch and test features in weeks.
Branches: convert the 10 lowest-traffic branches into advice centers for mortgages, small business and planning instead of closing them outright.
Visual: a before-and-after org chart and a timeline of feature launches.

Judge Q1: Copy what customers value, not the whole model. Fintechs win on convenience, like early direct deposit and instant transfers, so we'd match those. But our profit comes from lending and relationships, so we'd build on that with fast loans and real advisors fintechs can't offer.

Judge Q2: Not if we do it carefully. We'd convert, not close, the lowest-traffic branches into advice centers, keep the busiest branches full-service and offer older customers one-on-one help with the app. Loyal customers keep their relationship, and the bank cuts costs.

cases.title: Automation at a unionized factory
cases.judge: CFO of a mid-sized auto parts manufacturer
cases.situation: The CFO (judge) of a manufacturer with 220 union employees wants a $3 million loan for robotic welding equipment. The union contract expires in 14 months, and workers worry the robots will replace jobs. The company's output per worker has been flat for three years while wages rose. A competitor that automated last year now underbids the company on contracts. The CFO asks whether the investment makes sense and how to handle the workforce.
tasks: How productivity affects the company's competitiveness
Specialization and division of labor on the production line
Organized labor and the upcoming contract
The law of diminishing returns
Business risks in the investment
questions: Won't this loan just pay for robots that replace my workers?
What happens to the loan if the union goes on strike next year?
model: Open: 'Flat productivity while wages rise is squeezing your margin. This investment is about staying competitive, and keeping the workforce on board is part of the plan.'

Productivity (EC:013): output per worker has been flat, so unit labor costs rise every year. Nationally, productivity rose 3.6% at an annual rate in Q3 2026 (BLS) as firms invested; the competitor's automation is why it can underbid.
Diminishing returns (EC:023): adding workers to the same lines adds less and less output. The fix is capital: welding robots expand the fixed input.
Specialization (EC:014): robots take repetitive welding; workers specialize in programming, maintenance and quality control, with higher skills and pay.

Organized labor (EC:015): involve the union early. Offer paid retraining, no layoffs from automation during the contract (reductions through retirements and turnover) and a share of productivity gains. Union membership is 10% nationally, but much higher in manufacturing communities, and a strike is a real risk.

Risk (EC:011): technology risk (installation delays), human risk (strike), economic risk (auto demand falls in a recession). Mitigations: vendor performance guarantees, phased installation and a covenant to hold cash reserves.
Loan structure: a 7-year equipment loan, secured by the equipment, fixed rate, sized so payments stay under 40% of the projected savings.
Visual: a chart of unit labor cost before and after automation and a timeline aligned to the contract expiration.

Judge Q1: It pays for equipment that makes your workers more productive. With robots handling repetitive welding, your people move into programming, maintenance and quality roles. We'd recommend committing to no automation layoffs during the contract, using retirements and turnover instead, and funding retraining. That protects jobs and your competitiveness.

Judge Q2: We'd plan for it. The loan would include a cash-reserve requirement covering at least three months of payments, and phasing the installation means the biggest spending comes after the new contract is signed. Bringing the union in now, with retraining and a share of the savings, makes a strike much less likely.

cases.title: A college student eyeing emerging markets
cases.judge: 20-year-old college student with a new Roth IRA
cases.situation: A 20-year-old college student (judge) has $6,000 in a new Roth IRA and read that India is one of the fastest-growing major economies. The student wants to put the whole account into an India stock fund, and also asked a friend about buying shares in a single Chinese company. The student's grandparents emigrated from a country that went through a currency crisis, and the family still keeps cash at home.
tasks: How a country's economic development affects investing
How globalization connects markets
The political environment and investment risk
How history shapes saving and investing habits
Comparing economic systems
questions: Why shouldn't I put everything in India if it's growing the fastest?
My family keeps cash at home because banks failed in their country. Are they wrong?
model: Open: 'Starting a Roth IRA at 20 is a great move. Let's make sure the money grows without one country's problems wiping it out.'
Development (EC:116): emerging markets like India grow faster than developed economies, with young populations, but carry more volatility, weaker currencies and less investor protection.
Globalization (EC:109): U.S. companies make up about 60% of world stock value; international funds give exposure to the other 40%, including emerging markets.
Political risk (EC:113): single-country bets can fail suddenly; investors in Russian stocks couldn't sell after 2022 sanctions.
Economic systems (EC:007): China's large state-owned sector means the government can change the rules for companies, so a single Chinese stock carries extra political and system risk.
Recommendation: about 60% U.S. total market index, 30% developed international, 10% emerging markets, all low-cost index funds. Rebalance once a year. Keep investing monthly.
History (EC:115): the family's habit comes from real experience; in the U.S., FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 and no depositor has lost insured money since 1933.
Visual: pie chart of the recommended mix and a growth chart of $100 a month from age 20 to 65.

Judge Q1: Because fast GDP growth doesn't guarantee strong stock returns, and one country can hit a political or currency crisis. A diversified mix with about 10% in emerging markets, including India, lets you benefit from that growth while U.S. and developed-market funds keep the account steady.

Judge Q2: They're responding to real history, so it makes sense they'd be cautious. But in the U.S., FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000 per bank, and no one has lost insured money since 1933. Cash at home can be stolen or lose value to inflation. A good first step is an insured high-yield savings account.

cases.title: Sourcing abroad without crossing the line
cases.judge: owner of a growing clothing brand
cases.situation: The owner (judge) of a 15-employee clothing brand plans to move production to a factory in Southeast Asia to cut costs by 30%. During a video call, a local agent hinted that a 'customs fee' paid to an official would speed up export permits. The owner has never worked with an overseas factory, the agent's emails sometimes ask to change bank account details, and the factory is in a region that floods during monsoon season.
tasks: The law and ethics of bribery and foreign payments
Cultural and social factors in overseas business
How geography affects the supply chain
Risks of electronic communication with overseas partners
Protecting the company's reputation
questions: Everyone says small payments are just how business works there. Why can't I pay it?
How do I know the person emailing me is really the factory's agent?
model: Open: 'Cutting costs 30% could transform your brand. Let's make sure it doesn't come with legal or reputational risks that cost more than it saves.'

Bribery (EC:140): the FCPA makes paying a foreign official to win or speed up business a federal crime for U.S. companies anywhere. The narrow facilitation exception is risky; many companies ban all such payments. Siemens paid about $1.6 billion in 2008 to settle bribery charges.
Response: decline, document the request, use a licensed customs broker and official channels, and get a written anti-bribery clause in the agent contract.

Culture (EC:110, EC:045): build the relationship with the factory owner directly, visit in person, respect local holidays in production schedules, and check labor practices, since customers care about fair treatment of workers.
Geography (EC:114): monsoon flooding is a supply risk. Schedule production around the season, hold extra inventory before it and identify a backup factory in another region.

Electronic communication (EC:111): requests to change bank details are classic business email compromise, which cost U.S. victims about $2.8 billion in 2024 (FBI). Verify every payment change by calling a known phone number, and use secure portals.
Reputation: audit the factory (labor, safety), keep records and include ethical sourcing in the brand story.
Visual: a risk matrix (likelihood vs impact) covering bribery, flooding, email fraud and quality.

Judge Q1: Because U.S. law applies to your company everywhere. Under the FCPA, paying an official to speed up business can bring fines and even prison, and customers may abandon a brand caught bribing. We'd use a licensed customs broker, document the request and plan for permits to take a little longer.

Judge Q2: Don't trust email alone. Any request to change payment details should be confirmed by calling the agent at a phone number you already have, not one in the email. Business email compromise cost U.S. victims about $2.8 billion in 2024, so we'd set a rule: no payment changes without a call-back and a second approval.

cases.title: A new hire worried about layoffs
cases.judge: 24-year-old in their first full-time job
cases.situation: A 24-year-old client (judge) started a $58,000-a-year job at a home-building company six months ago. News about rising interest rates and the client's company slowing hiring has the client worried about layoffs. The client has $2,500 in savings, a $14,000 car loan, and asks whether to take a second job or go back to school for a certificate in a growing field. The client wants to understand how the economy affects their job.
tasks: How business cycles affect different industries
What the unemployment rate means for the client
Consumer spending as a signal for the economy
Economic resources, including human capital
Opportunities in a private enterprise system
questions: Is my job safe if the economy slows down?
Should I go back to school or take a second job?
model: Open: 'It's smart to think about this now, while you're employed. Let's build a cushion and a plan so a slowdown doesn't become a crisis.'

Business cycle (EC:018): home building is a cyclical industry; it's sensitive to interest rates (30-year mortgages near 7.11% in Nov. 2026, Freddie Mac). In downturns, cyclical industries cut jobs first.
Unemployment (EC:082): unemployment is 4.1% (Oct. 2026), a fairly healthy level, but layoffs happen even in expansions; structural and cyclical unemployment hit specific industries.
Consumer spending (EC:081): real spending was nearly flat in September 2026 and sentiment is low, so the client should prepare even though the economy is still growing.
Plan: (1) build the emergency fund to three months of expenses (about $9,000), then six; (2) keep the car loan current and avoid new debt; (3) keep contributing enough to get the full 401(k) match.

Human capital (EC:003): a certificate in a growing field raises earning power. In 2024, workers with more education earned more and had lower unemployment (BLS). Check if the employer offers tuition assistance.
Private enterprise (EC:009): the client can also earn side income through freelancing or a small business, which diversifies income.
Visual: a timeline of the emergency fund growing month by month, plus a chart of unemployment rates by education level.

Judge Q1: No job is completely safe, and home building tends to slow when rates are high. But unemployment is 4.1%, so jobs are still fairly available. The best protection is a cushion: three to six months of expenses saved, low debt and up-to-date skills, so a layoff would be a setback, not a crisis.

Judge Q2: Start with the savings cushion, then add skills. A part-time job or freelancing for a few months can fund the emergency fund faster. After that, a certificate in a growing field builds human capital, which raises earnings and job security. Check first whether your employer offers tuition help.

cases.judge: 22-year-old client starting a first full-time job
cases.situation: A 22-year-old client (judge) just started a $52,000-a-year job as a junior accountant. The employer offers a 401(k) with a 100% match on the first 4% of salary. The client has $24,000 in federal student loans at 5.5%, a $3,200 credit card balance at 24% APR and $600 in savings. Friends keep talking about buying individual stocks and crypto, and the client feels behind. The client (judge) wants a plan for the first year of real income.
tasks: Why saving and investing early matters
Types of investments and which fit a beginner
How retirement accounts and the employer match work
Using credit wisely while paying down debt
questions: Should I pay off my student loans before I invest anything?
How do I know if an investment tip from a friend is a scam?
model: Open: "In 12 months you'll have zero credit card debt, a starter emergency fund and a retirement account growing on autopilot."
Client service (CR:012): we learned your goals first, we'll explain how we're paid, and we act in your best interest. You can look us up on FINRA BrokerCheck.
Order of operations: 1) contribute 4% to get the full match, which is an instant 100% return. 2) Wipe out the 24% card (avalanche). 3) Build 3 months of expenses. 4) Raise 401(k) 1% each raise.
Need to save and invest (FI:270): $200 a month from 22 to 65 at an 8% average return grows to roughly $895,000. Starting at 32 gives about $387,000, less than half. Time is the advantage.

Types of investments (FI:077): stocks (ownership, higher return and risk), bonds (loans, steadier), index funds and target-date funds (instant diversification, expense ratios often under 0.10%). Crypto and single stocks only with money you can lose, under 5%.
Retirement (FI:569): traditional 401(k) lowers taxes now; a Roth IRA (2026 limit $7,500) grows tax-free, great while your tax bracket is low.
Credit (FI:071): pay the card in full by autopay, keep utilization under 30%, never close your oldest card. Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score.
Automate: split direct deposit so savings and investing happen before you can spend it. Review every 6 months.
Judge Q1: no. Federal loans at 5.5% are moderate, so get the match first, kill the 24% card, then split extra money between loans and investing.
Judge Q2: red flags are guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, and unregistered sellers. Check the SEC's Investor.gov and FINRA BrokerCheck.
cases.title: First paycheck plan

cases.judge: married client expecting twins
cases.situation: A married client (judge), age 31, and spouse are expecting twins in four months. Household income is $118,000. They rent, have $9,000 in savings, no life insurance outside a small policy through work, and no wills. They want to buy a home in three years and are worried about the cost of college for two children at once.
tasks: Setting financial goals for a growing family
Insurance needs for new parents
Options for financing college
How the time value of money affects their plan
Building trust in the advisor relationship
questions: What if one of us wants to stay home with the babies for a year?
Which should come first: the house or college savings?
model: Build trust (EI:128): start by listening, restate their goals back to them, explain fees in plain terms and promise a written plan with no surprises.
Goals (FI:065), SMART: emergency fund to 6 months ($30,000) in 18 months; $45,000 house down payment in 3 years; college savings starting the month the twins are born.

Insurance (FI:571): term life on BOTH parents, about 10 to 12 times income, 20-to-30-year term (inexpensive for healthy 31-year-olds); long-term disability insurance; add the twins to health insurance within the special enrollment window; write wills that name a guardian.

College (FI:831): open a 529 plan for each twin; growth is tax-free for qualified education costs. Unused money can move to a sibling, and up to $35,000 lifetime can roll into the child's Roth IRA (SECURE 2.0 rules). Babies born 2025-2028 can also get a $1,000 federal seed deposit in a Trump Account.
TVM (FI:062): $150 a month per twin from birth at 6% grows to about $58,000 each by 18. Starting at age 10 instead takes about $473 a month, more than three times as much, to reach the same amount.
Order: emergency fund and insurance first (protect), then 401(k) match, then 529 and house fund in parallel.
Automate everything on payday; review the plan at each life event and once a year.
Judge Q1: build a one-income budget now and live on it, banking the second income. That trial run proves it works and grows the fund.
Judge Q2: protect first, then both at a smaller scale. You can borrow for college but you can't borrow for retirement, and a house fund needs safety (high-yield savings or CDs), not stocks.
cases.title: Twins on the way

cases.judge: client who just inherited $180,000
cases.situation: A 44-year-old client (judge) inherited $180,000 from a parent. The client has a $210,000 mortgage at 3.1%, $11,000 in car loans, a modest 401(k) and two teenagers. Since the news spread, relatives have asked for loans and a 'friend of a friend' pitched a private real estate deal promising 18% guaranteed returns. The client (judge) feels overwhelmed and wants guidance.
tasks: Types of investments available for a lump sum
Types of financial markets and institutions involved
Legal protections and warning signs of fraud
Planning for the client's own estate
questions: Should I just pay off my mortgage?
How much of this can I give my kids without problems?
model: Open with a pause: park the money in an FDIC-insured high-yield savings account or Treasury bills for 60 to 90 days while we build the plan. No rushed decisions.
Fraud (BL:133): 'guaranteed 18%' is the top red flag of a Ponzi scheme. Madoff's fraud promised steady returns too. Check any seller and offering on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's EDGAR database.
Plan: pay off the $11,000 car loans (guaranteed return), top off a 6-month emergency fund, max retirement accounts, invest the rest in a diversified low-cost index portfolio.
Types of investments (FI:077): stocks, bonds, index funds, CDs, Treasuries, REITs. Match each to a goal and time horizon.

Markets (FI:337): money market for the parking spot, capital market for long-term stocks and bonds. Institutions (FI:336): FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor per bank; SIPC covers up to $500,000 at a brokerage if the firm fails, not market losses.
Mortgage at 3.1%: keep it. Long-run stock returns have averaged around 10% a year, and safe yields are near 4% today, so paying off cheap debt early gives up growth.
Estate (FI:572): update the will, name beneficiaries on every account, consider a revocable trust for the teens.
Family loans: set a 'gift budget' you can afford to never see again, and say 'my advisor manages this' to take the pressure off.
Judge Q1: no, at 3.1% the mortgage is cheap money. Paying it off locks $180,000 into one illiquid asset.
Judge Q2: in 2026 you can give up to $19,000 per person per year without filing a gift tax return. Fund a 529 or a custodial Roth IRA if a teen has earned income.
cases.title: The $180,000 inheritance

cases.judge: 58-year-old couple behind on retirement savings
cases.situation: A couple (judge), both 58, has $140,000 in retirement savings, a paid-off home and a combined income of $135,000. They spent years paying for their children's college and now fear they cannot retire at 65. They are nervous about the stock market after recent swings, and they watched one parent spend heavily on nursing-home care.
tasks: Retirement planning for late starters
How economic conditions affect financial markets
Calculating the effect of time and interest
Insurance needs before and during retirement
The advisor's responsibilities to the clients
questions: Is it too late for us to invest in stocks?
What happens to our plan if there's a recession right when we retire?
model: Client responsibilities (CR:012): we'll act as fiduciaries, put recommendations in writing and explain every fee.
Catch-up power (FI:569): in 2027 each can put $25,500 plus an $8,500 catch-up into a 401(k), and $7,500 plus $1,100 into an IRA. Ages 60 to 63 get a higher 401(k) catch-up of $11,750.
TVM (FI:238): saving $3,000 a month for 7 years at 6% adds about $310,000. With the $140,000 growing too, they could reach about $520,000 by 65.
Social Security: waiting from 62 to 70 raises the monthly check substantially (about 8% for each year past full retirement age). Use ssa.gov to get real estimates.

Economic conditions (FI:574): recessions push stock prices down, but the market has recovered from every past bear market. The Fed raised rates in September 2026 to fight inflation near 3.7%, which also means safe bonds and CDs pay more right now.
Mix: a balanced portfolio (about 60% stocks and 40% bonds), shifting gradually. Keep 2 years of spending in cash and bonds at retirement so they never sell stocks in a crash.
Insurance (FI:571): look at long-term care insurance now, while they're healthy and premiums are lower; keep disability coverage until retirement; umbrella liability.
Downsizing the paid-off home later is a backup source of money.
Judge Q1: no. At 65 their money may need to last 25 to 30 years, so some stocks are needed to beat inflation.
Judge Q2: the 2-year cash bucket covers spending while stocks recover, and working part-time or delaying Social Security adds flexibility.
cases.title: Retirement at 58: catching up

cases.judge: chef who wants to launch a food truck
cases.situation: A talented chef (judge) wants to leave a restaurant job to open a food truck selling Korean-Mexican fusion tacos. The chef has $25,000 saved, found a used truck for $68,000, and plans to work with a cousin who would handle social media and events. The chef (judge) has no business experience and asked for the basics.
tasks: What it means to be an entrepreneur
Types of business ownership for the chef and cousin
Building a start-up and operating budget
Overhead and operating costs to expect
Insurance needs for a food truck
questions: How long until I can pay myself a salary?
How will I know early if the business is in trouble?
model: Entrepreneurship (EN:039): you carry the risk and the reward. The Bureau of Labor Statistics finds about 1 in 5 new businesses close in the first year, usually from cash problems, not bad food.

Ownership (BL:003): an LLC with a written operating agreement that spells out who owns what, who decides and what happens if one partner leaves. It protects personal assets and passes profits through for taxes.
Financing: SBA microloans go up to $50,000, and SBA 7(a) loans are larger. Equipment financing on the truck uses the truck as collateral.
Budget (FI:106): start-up costs (truck, wrap, equipment, permits, first inventory) plus a monthly operating budget with best, expected and worst-case sales.
Overhead (OP:024): commissary kitchen rent, fuel, propane, permits and health inspections, POS fees (about 2.6% to 3% per card swipe), insurance, truck maintenance.
Break-even: with $9,000 in monthly fixed costs and $6 of profit per $12 taco plate, you need 1,500 plates a month, about 70 a day on 22 service days.
Insurance (FI:571): commercial auto, general liability, product liability (food illness), equipment coverage, and workers' comp if you hire.
Set up a separate business bank account and cloud bookkeeping (QuickBooks or Xero) from day one.
Judge Q1: pay yourself a small fixed draw only after 3 months of operating costs are in reserve, often 6 to 12 months in.
Judge Q2: watch weekly cash flow and plates sold against break-even. Two weeks below break-even means change the location or menu.
cases.title: Launching a food truck

cases.role: credit counselors at a credit union
cases.judge: young couple with credit card debt who want to buy a home
cases.situation: A couple in their late 20s (judge) earns $86,000 combined. They have $16,500 in credit card debt across four cards (APRs from 19% to 29%), one card that was 60 days late last spring, and credit scores around 610. They want to buy a $300,000 home in two years. A company on social media offered to 'erase their bad credit' for $899.
tasks: Controlling and paying down debt
Checking and correcting their credit history
Calculating the real cost of their credit
Building a personal budget that supports their goal
The purposes and importance of credit
questions: Should we close the credit cards once they're paid off?
Would a debt consolidation loan help us?
model: Cost of credit (FI:782): $16,500 at about 24% costs roughly $330 a month in interest alone. Paying only minimums could take more than 15 years.
Budget (FI:066): track one month of spending, then a zero-based budget. Put $900 a month toward the cards and they're gone in about 23 months, sooner if the issuers cut the rates.
Debt plan (FI:568): avalanche (highest APR first) saves the most money; snowball (smallest balance first) gives quick wins. Call each issuer and ask for a lower rate.
Credit history (FI:072): pull all three reports free at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors yourself for free. 'Credit repair' companies cannot legally remove accurate negative information.
Why credit matters (FI:002): on a $300,000 mortgage, a score in the 600s vs the high 700s can mean a much higher rate, tens of thousands of dollars over 30 years.
Score levers: payment history (35%) through autopay on everything; utilization (30%), getting under 30% and ideally under 10%. Late payments fade in impact over time.
Home timeline: aim for a score above 700, debt-to-income under 36%, and an FHA loan needs as little as 3.5% down.
Judge Q1: keep them open with a small autopaid bill. Closing cards lowers available credit and shortens credit history.
Judge Q2: only if the new rate is clearly lower, there are no big fees, and they freeze the cards so they don't run them up again.
cases.title: Credit comeback before a first home

cases.role: marketing manager and digital banking manager
cases.judge: president of a community bank losing young customers
cases.situation: HOMETOWN BANK (judge: bank president) has 22 branches, but only 8% of its customers are under 30, and young customers leave for app-only banks and payment apps. The bank's app has a 2.9-star rating. The president (judge) wants a plan to attract and keep customers ages 18 to 29 while protecting the bank's reputation for safety.
tasks: The role of financial institutions compared with fintech apps
Using CRM technology to understand young customers
Helping customers manage online accounts securely
Protecting customers against identity theft and scams
Communicating with a young target audience
questions: How will we measure whether this works?
Why would a young person choose us over a free app?
model: Role of institutions (FI:336): unlike many apps, Hometown is FDIC-insured to $250,000 and can lend. The 2024 collapse of fintech middleman Synapse froze customers' money, which is a story to tell.
Fix the app first: instant transfers through FedNow or Zelle, early direct deposit, round-up savings, card freeze button, spending insights.
CRM (CR:024): segment by life stage (first job, college, first apartment) and trigger offers like a first-car loan pre-approval when a customer's direct deposit starts.
Online accounts (FI:830): multifactor authentication, biometric login, alerts on every transaction.
Identity theft (FI:073): in-app scam warnings before first-time payments; teach credit freezes. The FTC reported consumers lost about $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024.
Communication (CO:084): short video on TikTok and Instagram, a student ambassador program at local colleges, plain-language money tips, never jargon.
Product: a no-fee 'First Account' bundle (checking, high-yield savings, credit-builder loan) plus free financial literacy workshops in high schools.
Judge Q1: KPIs are accounts opened under 30, app rating (target 4.5), 90-day retention, products per young customer.
Judge Q2: safety (FDIC insurance), a real person when something goes wrong, and a credit-builder path to a first car or home loan, which apps can't match.
cases.title: HOMETOWN BANK wins Gen Z

cases.judge: CEO of a credit union
cases.situation: LAKESHORE CREDIT UNION (judge: CEO) has 60,000 members. Most keep money in basic savings earning 0.25%, even though the credit union pays 4.10% APY on a 12-month share certificate (its version of a CD) with a $500 minimum. With inflation running well above 3%, the CEO (judge) wants an informational campaign that helps members understand why idle savings lose value and how to use certificates and money market accounts.
tasks: The need to save and invest
Types of financial markets and savings products
Why delaying is a lost opportunity (time value of money)
How economic conditions affect rates
Writing a clear informational message
questions: Are there any disadvantages to a share certificate?
Which channel is best to reach our members?
model: Message (CO:039): headline 'Your savings deserve a raise.' Short, plain words, one example, one call to action.
Need to save (FI:270): at 0.25% with inflation near 3.7%, $10,000 loses about $345 of buying power in a year. At 4.10% it keeps pace and grows.

Products and markets (FI:337): savings (flexible, low rate), money market account (higher rate, some limits), share certificate (fixed rate for a term, penalty for early withdrawal). These live in the money market for short-term funds.
TVM (FI:062): $10,000 at 4.10% earns $410 in a year vs $25 at 0.25%. Waiting six months to move the money gives up about $190.
Economy (FI:574): the Fed raised its rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026 to fight inflation, which is why certificate rates are high now. Locking a 12-month rate protects members if rates fall.
Ladder idea: split savings into 3-, 6- and 12-month certificates so some money comes free every few months.
Safety: NCUA insures credit union deposits up to $250,000, the same protection as FDIC.
Channels: app banner and push notice, statement insert, teller talking points, short social video, email to members with over $5,000 in savings.
Judge Q1: money is locked until maturity and early withdrawal costs some interest; if rates rise further, you're stuck at the old rate (a ladder helps).
Judge Q2: the app and email, because they're personal and trackable, backed by teller conversations for members who prefer branches.
cases.title: LAKESHORE CREDIT UNION savings campaign

cases.judge: owner of a landscaping company
cases.situation: GREENEDGE LANDSCAPING (judge: owner) earns 80% of its $900,000 yearly revenue from April through October. Every winter the company struggles to make payroll for its six year-round employees and has paid late fees on equipment loans. The owner checks the bank balance daily but has no budget. The owner (judge) wants to fix the winter cash crunch.
tasks: Reading the cash flow statement
Building budgets for a seasonal business
Using budgeting technology
Using credit wisely for working capital
Controlling business risks
questions: Why can we be profitable and still run out of cash?
What should I do with extra cash in a great summer?
model: Cash flow (FI:091): profit isn't cash. Operating cash peaks in summer; investing (equipment) and financing (loan payments) outflows continue all year.
Cash budget (FI:106): a 12-month cash flow budget by month shows the gap. If winter costs run $45,000 a month for 5 months, they need a $225,000 cushion.
Technology (FM:013): QuickBooks Online or Xero with bank feeds, plus a rolling 13-week cash forecast. Run what-if scenarios for a rainy summer.
Credit (FI:002): a business line of credit set up while finances look strong in summer. Draw in winter, repay in spring. It's cheaper than late fees.
Smooth revenue: prepaid annual maintenance contracts with a small discount, snow removal and holiday lighting in winter.
Risk control (RM:058): require deposits on big jobs, invoice within 24 hours, offer card and ACH payment, and set a cash reserve policy.
Ratio to watch: current ratio above 1.5 going into November.
Judge Q1: revenue is recorded when earned, but customers pay late and loan payments don't stop in winter. Timing creates the gap.
Judge Q2: build the winter reserve first, pay down the line of credit, then invest in equipment that wins new contracts.
cases.title: GREENEDGE LANDSCAPING's winter cash crunch

cases.judge: longtime customer whose identity was stolen
cases.situation: A 67-year-old customer (judge) of 30 years got a call from someone claiming to be from the bank's fraud department and shared a one-time passcode. Within an hour, $8,400 was transferred out through a payment app, and a credit card was opened in the customer's name. The customer (judge) is embarrassed, angry at the bank and thinking of moving all accounts elsewhere.
tasks: Protecting against identity theft
Checking and validating credit history
Managing online accounts safely
The responsibilities of finance professionals to clients
Showing empathy for the customer
questions: Will I get my money back?
How do I know a call is really from the bank?
model: Empathy (EI:030): 'This is not your fault. These criminals are professionals and they target everyone.' Listen first, then act.
Responsibilities (CR:012): we'll open a fraud claim today, freeze affected accounts, give you one point of contact and follow up in writing.
Identity theft steps (FI:073): report at IdentityTheft.gov (FTC) for a recovery plan, freeze credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion (free), file a police report, close the fraudulent card.
Credit history (FI:072): check all three reports at AnnualCreditReport.com (free weekly) and dispute the fake account.
Online accounts (FI:830): new passwords, an authenticator app instead of text codes, alerts on every transfer, a lower daily transfer limit.
Golden rule: the bank will never call and ask for a passcode. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.
Prevention: a trusted-contact person on the account and a verbal password with the bank.
Older adults are top targets: the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center reported people 60 and over lost about $4.9 billion to fraud in 2024.

Judge Q1: under federal Regulation E, transfers a criminal makes count as unauthorized, and reporting quickly limits what you can lose. We'll investigate and keep you updated. The fake card isn't your debt.
Judge Q2: hang up, call the number on your card or statement, and never share codes. Caller ID can be faked.
cases.title: After the phone scam

cases.judge: recently divorced single parent of two
cases.situation: A 38-year-old client (judge) finalized a divorce two months ago and now supports two children, ages 6 and 10, on a $64,000 salary plus $900 a month in child support. The client kept the house (a $1,450 monthly mortgage payment), has $4,000 in savings and a 401(k) worth $38,000. The client's ex-spouse is still listed as the beneficiary on the 401(k) and a work life insurance policy. The client has never managed the household budget alone and feels anxious about money for the first time.
tasks: Building a budget on one income
Setting financial goals for the next three years
Insurance needs as the sole provider
Estate planning steps after a divorce
How the advisors will earn the client's trust
questions: What happens to my kids financially if something happens to me tomorrow?
Should I sell the house to have more breathing room?
model: Open with empathy and trust (EI:128): 'Lots of families go through this, and you're doing the right thing by planning now.' Explain how we're paid, and that you'll get a written plan with no surprises.

Budget (FI:066): start from net income (salary take-home plus $900 child support), list fixed costs first (mortgage, insurance, childcare), then variable. Use 50/30/20 as a guide, but housing alone may be above 30%, so trim wants first.

Goals (FI:065), SMART: $1,000 starter emergency fund in 60 days; 3 months of expenses (about $12,000) in 18 months; keep the full 401(k) match every paycheck; start a 529 for each child at $50 a month.

Insurance (FI:571): as the only earner, term life of about 10 to 12 times income (20-year term covers both kids to adulthood) and long-term disability insurance replacing about 60% of pay. About 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before retirement age (SSA).

Estate (FI:572), urgent: beneficiary designations override a will, so the ex-spouse would still receive the 401(k) and life insurance today. Update every beneficiary form this week, write a will naming a guardian, and set up a trust or custodian so the kids' money is managed until adulthood.
Protect the income: confirm health insurance for the kids, and keep child support in a separate account tracked against the budget.
Automate: transfer savings the day after payday so it happens before spending. Review the plan in six months and at each life change.
Visual to hand the judge: a one-page budget pie (needs / wants / savings) and a 3-year timeline of the goals.

Judge Q1: Today, the 401(k) and work policy would go to your ex-spouse because of the old beneficiary forms, so we fix that first. With updated beneficiaries, a will naming a guardian, a trust for the kids and a term life policy, they'd have money for housing and college managed by someone you choose.

Judge Q2: Not yet. Selling has costs (often 6% to 10% with agent fees and moving) and uproots the kids. Let's run the budget for three months. If housing stays above about 35% of take-home pay and savings can't grow, then downsizing becomes the right move, and we'd plan it carefully.
cases.title: Single parent: starting over

cases.judge: full-time rideshare driver and freelance designer
cases.situation: A 27-year-old client (judge) earns money three ways: rideshare driving, freelance graphic design and tips from weekend catering work. Income swings from $2,800 to $6,000 a month and totaled about $52,000 last year. Nothing is withheld for taxes, and the client owed $4,100 in April with a penalty. The client has no retirement account, no health insurance through an employer and $1,800 in savings. The client wants stability without giving up the freedom of gig work.
tasks: Sources of income and how each is taxed
Budgeting with irregular income
Preparing for income taxes
Retirement options for the self-employed
Insurance needs for gig workers
questions: How much should I set aside for taxes from each payment?
Is it worth getting a regular part-time job just for the benefits?
model: Open: 'You can keep your freedom and still get a paycheck-like system. We'll build it around your lowest month.'

Income (FI:061): driving and design are self-employment income (1099-NEC/1099-K); catering tips are tip income. Under the 2025 tax law, up to $25,000 of qualified tips is deductible from federal income tax for 2025-2028, but payroll taxes still apply.

Taxes (FI:067): self-employment tax is 15.3% (Social Security + Medicare, both halves) on net earnings, plus income tax. Pay quarterly estimated taxes (April, June, September, January) to avoid penalties. Track mileage and business expenses, which lower taxable profit on Schedule C.

Budget (FI:066): budget from the lowest typical month ($2,800). Every payment goes into one 'income' account; pay yourself a fixed salary from it; extra in good months goes to a buffer that covers slow months.
Account system: (1) income account, (2) tax account, 25% to 30% of every payment moved automatically, (3) bills, (4) buffer and emergency fund.

Retirement (FI:569): a SEP-IRA or Solo 401(k) lets self-employed people save much more than a regular IRA. A Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026 and 2027) is great while income is moderate. Starting in 2027, the Saver's Match can add up to $1,000 a year for eligible savers.

Insurance (FI:571): health insurance through the HealthCare.gov marketplace (a high-deductible plan with an HSA can work), disability coverage, and confirm rideshare insurance, since personal auto policies often exclude driving for an app.
Visual: a flow diagram showing each payment splitting into tax, bills, buffer and savings.

Judge Q1: Move 25% to 30% of every payment into a separate tax account the day it arrives. That covers 15.3% self-employment tax plus income tax at your level. Then pay quarterly estimates from that account so April has no surprises and no penalty.

Judge Q2: Only if the benefits are worth more than the time. Employer health insurance can be worth thousands a year, and a 401(k) match is free money. Compare that against what you'd earn in the same hours driving or designing. If marketplace coverage is affordable for you, the freedom may be worth more.
cases.title: Gig worker: steady pay from unsteady income

cases.judge: newly married couple combining finances
cases.situation: Newlyweds (judge), both 29, just combined households. One spouse earns $71,000, has a 790 credit score and $22,000 saved. The other earns $56,000, has a 640 credit score after missed payments in college, $14,000 in credit card debt and no savings. They argue about money and want to buy a home within two years. They don't know whether to combine all their accounts or keep them separate.
tasks: Setting shared financial goals
How credit history affects borrowing
Applying for a mortgage
Why saving and investing matter for their future
The advisors' responsibilities to both spouses
questions: Should we combine all our money into joint accounts?
Should we apply for the mortgage using only the spouse with the better credit?
model: Responsibilities (CR:012): we work for both of you equally, keep everything confidential and explain every option and its cost.
Goals (FI:065): agree on shared SMART goals first: pay off the $14,000 card in 18 months, build a $15,000 emergency fund, and save a $30,000 down payment in 24 months.

Account structure: 'yours, mine and ours': a joint account for shared bills and goals, funded by each spouse in proportion to income (about 56% / 44%), plus personal spending money for each. It cuts arguments while keeping autonomy.

Credit history (FI:072): pull all three reports free at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors. Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score and utilization about 30%, so on-time autopay and paying the card down below 30% of its limit raise the 640 score fastest.

Mortgage (FI:625): lenders review credit, income (pay stubs, W-2s), debt-to-income ratio and down payment. 20% down avoids private mortgage insurance. Get pre-approved by 2-3 lenders within about two weeks so inquiries count as one.

Save and invest (FI:270): the down payment belongs in a high-yield savings account or CDs (top accounts paid about 4.35% APY in Nov. 2026) because it's needed in two years. Retirement money stays invested in index funds for growth.
Avalanche the 24% card first: at about 22% average card rates, paying it off is a guaranteed return better than any investment.
Visual: a side-by-side timeline: months 1-18 debt payoff, months 1-24 down payment growth, credit score milestones.

Judge Q1: Combine the shared part. A joint account for bills and goals, each contributing by income share, plus a personal account each for guilt-free spending. Couples who agree on a system argue less, and you both see progress toward the house.

Judge Q2: Possibly. Applying on one income with the 790 score may get a better rate, but it limits how much you can borrow. Let's compare both ways at pre-approval. In 12 to 18 months of on-time payments and lower card balances, the 640 score could rise enough to apply jointly at a good rate.
cases.title: Newlyweds merge their money

cases.judge: parent of a 16-year-old starting a first job
cases.situation: A parent (judge) visits the bank with questions about their 16-year-old, who just got a part-time job at a grocery store earning $14 an hour for about 15 hours a week. The teen has never had a bank account and was confused by the first pay stub. The parent wants the teen to learn good money habits, avoid debt mistakes and start saving for college and a car, but worries about online scams and overspending on apps.
tasks: Reading a pay stub and understanding sources of income
Choosing a financial-services provider and account
Managing online accounts safely
The need to save and invest
The purposes and risks of credit
questions: Should my teen get a credit card now to start building credit?
How can my teen save for both a car and college on a small paycheck?
model: Open: 'Learning this at 16 is a huge head start. Habits built now last a lifetime.'

Pay stub (FI:068): gross pay ($14 x 15 = $210 a week), then deductions: federal and state income tax withholding (often small or none at this income, set by the W-4), Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% (FICA). Net pay is what lands in the account. Year-to-date totals help track earnings.
Taxes: a teen with withholding should still file a return, because tax withheld may be fully refunded if income is below the standard deduction ($16,100 single for 2026).

Choosing a provider (FI:076): compare fees, minimums, FDIC (bank) or NCUA (credit union) insurance up to $250,000, mobile app quality and parental controls. A teen checking account linked to a parent's account with no monthly fee fits best.

Online safety (FI:830): strong unique password, app-based two-factor login, transaction alerts, never share codes. Under Regulation E, reporting an unauthorized debit within 2 business days caps losses at $50.

Save and invest (FI:270): pay yourself first: split direct deposit so 30% goes straight to savings. A custodial Roth IRA is possible with earned income, and money invested at 16 has 50 years to compound.

Credit (FI:002): credit lets you buy now and pay later at a cost. Average card rates were about 22% in 2026. Building credit can start safely as an authorized user on a parent's card, with no debt risk to the teen.
Visual: a pie chart of one paycheck: spend / car fund / college fund / Roth IRA.

Judge Q1: Not on their own yet. Under-21 card applicants need independent income or a cosigner, and mistakes at 22% interest are expensive. Adding your teen as an authorized user on your card, with a small spending limit, builds their credit history safely, and you can watch the habits.

Judge Q2: Split every paycheck automatically into separate buckets, for example 20% car fund and 10% college or Roth IRA, both in a high-yield savings account. At about $190 a week net, that's roughly $57 a week saved, nearly $3,000 a year, plus interest.
cases.title: A teen's first paycheck

cases.judge: 63-year-old client panicking after a market drop
cases.situation: A 63-year-old client (judge) plans to retire in two years with $610,000 in a 401(k) that is 85% stocks. After a recent 14% market drop, the client called wanting to move everything to cash. The client expects about $2,600 a month from Social Security at full retirement age (67) and needs about $5,200 a month to live. The client remembers 2008 and is losing sleep.
tasks: How economic conditions affect financial markets
Planning retirement income
Types of investments for someone near retirement
Responding to the client's emotions with empathy
The advisor's responsibilities in a crisis
questions: What if the market keeps falling right after I retire?
When should I start taking Social Security?
model: Empathy first (EI:030): 'Losing sleep over this is completely understandable, especially after 2008. Let's look at what this drop actually means for your plan.'
Responsibilities (CR:012): we're acting in your best interest, which sometimes means advising against what feels urgent. Selling now locks in the loss.

Markets and the economy (FI:574): markets fall and recover with the business cycle. The S&P 500 fell about 37% in 2008 and 18% in 2022 and recovered both times. With GDP growing 3.4% last quarter and unemployment at 4.1%, the economy is still expanding.
The real issue: 85% stocks is too aggressive two years from retirement. Shift gradually toward about 50-60% stocks, with bonds and cash, rather than all at once in a panic.

Income plan (FI:569): need $5,200 a month; Social Security covers $2,600; the gap is $2,600 a month ($31,200 a year). At a 4% withdrawal rate, $610,000 supports about $24,400 a year, so we close the rest by working part-time briefly, delaying Social Security or trimming spending.

Bucket strategy (FI:077): bucket 1, two years of withdrawals in cash and short-term Treasuries; bucket 2, bonds for years 3-7; bucket 3, stock index funds for growth. Market drops never force selling stocks.
Sequence-of-returns risk: a crash early in retirement does the most damage, which is exactly what the cash bucket protects against.
Visual: a three-bucket diagram and a line chart of the S&P 500 recovering after 2008 and 2022.

Judge Q1: That's why we build the cash bucket now. With two years of spending in cash and Treasuries, you won't have to sell stocks in a downturn, giving them time to recover, as they did after 2008 and 2022.

Judge Q2: If you're healthy, waiting usually pays. Claiming at 62 cuts the benefit permanently by up to 30%, while each year after 67 adds 8% until 70. Since your Social Security covers half your needs, delaying even to 67 or 68 makes your guaranteed income bigger for life, and benefits rise with inflation (3.6% in 2027).
cases.title: Two years to retirement, then a market drop

cases.judge: talented baker starting a business with a friend
cases.situation: A client (judge) has baked custom cakes from home for three years and now wants to open a small bakery with a friend who has restaurant management experience. The client would contribute $25,000 and the friend $15,000. They found a storefront for $3,200 a month and estimate $85,000 in start-up costs for equipment, renovation and first inventory. Neither has owned a business, and they haven't decided how to split ownership or decisions.
tasks: The nature of entrepreneurship and what owners do
Types of business ownership for two partners
The role of finance in starting the business
Creating a start-up and operating budget
Insurance needs for a food business
questions: What happens to the business if my friend and I disagree or one of us wants out?
Where can we get the rest of the money we need?
model: Open: 'Three years of custom orders means you already have proof customers want what you make. Now let's build the business around it.'
Entrepreneurship (EN:039): owners take the risk and the reward. You'll lead the product; your partner's management experience covers operations. Divide roles in writing.

Ownership (BL:003): a general partnership is simple but each partner is personally liable for business debts. An LLC protects personal assets and passes profits through to your tax returns. Recommend an LLC with a written operating agreement covering ownership split, decisions, capital and buyouts.

Finance (FI:354): $40,000 contributed against $85,000 needed leaves a $45,000 gap, plus at least 3-6 months of operating reserve. Options: an SBA microloan (up to $50,000), an SBA 7(a) loan through a bank, equipment financing, or a small family investment.

Budget (FI:106): start-up budget (equipment, renovation, permits, deposit, opening inventory) and a monthly operating budget (rent $3,200, ingredients, payroll, utilities, insurance, loan payment). Find break-even: monthly fixed costs / contribution margin per sale.

Insurance (FI:571): general and product liability (food illness claims), commercial property for ovens and equipment, business interruption, workers' compensation once you hire, and a business owner's policy (BOP) to bundle coverage.
Test first: keep the custom-cake business running and add a weekend farmers' market booth to prove storefront demand before signing a long lease.
Visual: a break-even chart and a pie chart of start-up costs.

Judge Q1: Put it in the operating agreement now, while you're friends. Spell out who decides what, how disagreements are settled (for example a mediator), and a buy-sell clause that sets how one partner can buy out the other at a fair, pre-agreed valuation method. Clear rules protect the friendship and the business.

Judge Q2: An SBA microloan can cover up to $50,000, and SBA 7(a) loans through a bank go higher with a government guarantee. Lenders will want a business plan, cash flow projections and your personal investment, which you already have at $40,000. Equipment financing can cover the ovens, using the equipment as collateral.
cases.title: Two friends open a bakery

cases.judge: owner of a hair salon considering a second location
cases.situation: The owner (judge) of a profitable hair salon has steady clients and $210,000 in annual revenue, with net income of $34,000. A second location in a growing neighborhood would cost $120,000 to open and $9,500 a month to run. The owner has $45,000 in business savings and an offer from an investor willing to provide $80,000 in exchange for 30% of the whole business. The owner is excited but nervous about stretching too far.
tasks: The role of finance in an expansion decision
Reading the income statement to judge readiness
Budgeting for the new location
Marginal analysis of the expansion
Managing the risks of growth
questions: Should I take the investor's money or a bank loan?
How will I know if the second location is working?
model: Open: 'A profitable salon with loyal clients is the right foundation. The question is how to grow without risking what you've built.'
Income statement (FI:094): net margin is $34,000 / $210,000 = about 16%. Check which services drive profit and whether that margin holds without the owner working every chair.

Finance (FI:354): compare financing. The investor's $80,000 for 30% of the whole business values it at about $267,000, and gives away 30% of current profits forever. A bank or SBA loan keeps 100% ownership, but payments are due every month.

Budget (FM:013): build a 12-month cash budget for location 2: $9,500 monthly costs, a ramp-up of clients over 6 months, loan payments, and a 3-month reserve. Run what-if scenarios at 70%, 100% and 120% of expected bookings.

Marginal analysis (FI:659): compare the extra revenue the second location brings with its extra costs. Break-even = $9,500 / contribution per appointment; with a $40 contribution that's about 238 appointments a month.

Risk (SM:075): risks include slow client build-up, staffing, a lease too long to exit, and spreading the owner too thin. Reduce with a lease that has an exit option, hiring a manager, and pre-booking clients from the current salon's waitlist.
Recommendation: a smaller SBA loan plus $25,000 of savings, keeping full ownership, with a manager hired before opening.
Visual: a break-even chart and a 12-month cash flow line showing the ramp-up.

Judge Q1: For a profitable salon with predictable revenue, a loan is usually better: you keep 100% ownership, interest is tax-deductible, and once it's repaid it's gone. The investor would own 30% of both locations' profits forever. We'd only choose the investor if their expertise or network is worth that stake.

Judge Q2: Set targets before opening: break-even of about 238 appointments a month by month 6, rebooking above 60%, and staff costs under a set share of revenue. We'll review a budget-versus-actual report monthly; if it misses targets for three straight months, we adjust marketing, staffing or hours.
cases.title: Should the salon open a second location?

cases.judge: owner of a growing online clothing shop
cases.situation: The owner (judge) of an online clothing shop doubled sales to $480,000 last year but is constantly short of cash. The shop must pay suppliers 30 days after ordering, while marketplace payouts arrive 14 days after each sale and inventory sits for an average of 75 days. The owner has been covering gaps with a business credit card charging 24% APR and now owes $38,000. The owner tracks finances in a spreadsheet updated once a month.
tasks: Understanding the cash flow statement
The purposes and costs of business credit
Technology tools for accounting
Financial analysis of the shop's performance
How tax rules affect the business's choices
questions: How can I be growing so fast and still be out of cash?
Should I get a business line of credit to replace the credit card?
model: Open: 'Growing this fast is a good problem, but cash is the oxygen of a business. Let's fix the flow.'

Cash flow (FI:091): profit isn't cash. Cash goes out when inventory is bought and comes in only when it sells and is paid out. The cash conversion cycle is 75 days of inventory + 14 days to get paid - 30 days to pay suppliers = 59 days the shop is funding its own growth.
Fixes: shorten inventory days (order smaller batches more often, discount slow sellers), negotiate 45-60 day supplier terms, and offer pre-orders on new collections.

Credit (FI:002): credit lets a business bridge timing gaps, but at 24% the card costs about $9,100 a year in interest on $38,000. A bank or SBA line of credit typically costs far less and is designed for working capital.
Technology (FI:352): move from a monthly spreadsheet to cloud accounting (QuickBooks Online or Xero) connected to the bank and marketplace, for daily numbers and a 13-week cash forecast.
Financial analysis (FM:014): track gross margin by product, inventory turnover, and days of cash on hand. Benchmark against similar retailers to find slow products tying up cash.

Taxes (BL:134): interest on business debt is deductible, and with 100% bonus depreciation restored permanently by the 2025 law, qualifying equipment like a new packing system can be deducted in year one. Collect sales tax where the shop meets state thresholds (Wayfair, 2018).
Visual: a cash conversion cycle timeline showing the 59-day gap.

Judge Q1: Because every sale ties up cash for about two months before it comes back. You pay suppliers in 30 days, but inventory sits 75 days and payouts take 14 more. The faster you grow, the more cash gets locked in inventory. Shortening that cycle frees cash without slowing growth.

Judge Q2: Yes. A line of credit is built for exactly this timing gap, usually at a much lower rate than 24%, and you only pay interest on what you draw. Use it to pay off the card, then draw on it only for inventory and repay as sales come in. Set it up now, while sales look strong.
cases.title: Growing fast, out of cash

cases.role: bank marketing manager and branch manager
cases.judge: president of a community bank
cases.situation: The president (judge) of HARBORVIEW COMMUNITY BANK has noticed that local high school students are opening accounts with app-only fintech companies instead of the bank. The president wants your team to design a one-page brochure and a short in-school presentation promoting the bank's new teen checking and savings accounts, which have no monthly fees, a debit card, parental alerts and a savings account paying 4.00% APY on balances up to $1,000.
tasks: Forms of financial exchange teens will use
The role of financial institutions and deposit insurance
Managing online accounts safely
Why teens should save early
Writing a persuasive message for teens
questions: Why should a teen choose our bank instead of an app like Cash App?
What will make students actually read the brochure?
model: Open: 'We'll show students that a bank account can be as easy as an app, and safer.'

Forms of exchange (FI:058): cash, debit cards, mobile wallets, peer-to-peer payments, checks and direct deposit. Cash is now only about 1 in 7 consumer payments (Federal Reserve), so teens need digital tools.

Role of financial institutions (FI:336): banks keep money safe, make payments and lend. FDIC insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank. Some app balances depend on partner banks; the 2024 Synapse collapse locked app customers out of their money for months.
Online safety (FI:830): two-factor login, instant alerts, card lock in the app, and Regulation E: report an unauthorized debit within 2 business days and your loss is capped at $50.
Save early (FI:270): $1,000 at 4.00% earns $40 a year with no risk; saving $20 a week from 16 to 18 builds about $2,000 plus interest, a head start on a car or college.

Persuasive brochure (CO:031): lead with benefits, not features: 'Get paid faster with direct deposit,' 'Lock your card in one tap,' 'Your money is FDIC-insured.' Short headline, three bullet benefits, a QR code to open an account and a clear call to action.
Presentation: 10 minutes at school, a quick quiz with a prize, real teen scenarios (first paycheck, splitting pizza money), and a parent sign-up night.
Measure success: number of teen accounts opened, direct deposits set up and average savings balance after 6 months.

Judge Q1: Our accounts match the app experience (mobile deposit, instant payments, card controls) and add things apps often don't: FDIC insurance directly at our bank, a 4.00% savings rate, local branches and people who can help. And if an app's partner fails, as Synapse did in 2024, customers can lose access to their money.

Judge Q2: Make it about them, not the bank: a bold headline like 'Your first paycheck, upgraded,' three short benefits, real numbers, bright design and a QR code to sign up in minutes. Test a draft with a few students first and use their words.
cases.title: HARBORVIEW BANK teen accounts

cases.judge: CEO of a credit union
cases.situation: The CEO (judge) of RIVERBEND CREDIT UNION is worried that many members in their 30s and 40s have little or no retirement savings. The CEO wants your team to plan and present a free evening retirement seminar for members, explaining retirement accounts, Social Security and investing basics, and encouraging members to meet with the credit union's advisors.
tasks: Retirement planning and account types
Calculating the time value of money
Types of investments for retirement
The responsibilities of finance professionals to members
Delivering an effective oral presentation
questions: What should a 45-year-old with no savings do first?
How do we make sure members trust our advisors and don't feel sold to?
model: Open: 'One evening can change members' retirements. We'll make it simple, honest and action-focused.'

Retirement accounts (FI:569): 401(k)/403(b) with employer match (limit $24,500 in 2026, $25,500 in 2027; catch-up from 50), IRAs and Roth IRAs ($7,500 in 2026 and 2027), and starting in 2027 the Saver's Match of up to $1,000 for eligible savers. Social Security replaces only about 40% of average income.
Time value of money (FI:238): $300 a month at 7% for 30 years grows to about $366,000; the same $300 for 20 years grows to about $156,000. Waiting 10 years costs more than half. Show it on one slide.
