Investments (FI:077): stocks, bonds, index funds and target-date funds; low fees (index funds often under 0.10%) leave more money compounding.
Responsibilities (CR:012): put members' interests first, disclose how advisors are paid, explain options in plain language, keep information confidential.
Presentation (CO:025): open with a story or striking number, 3 key points, one simple chart per point, live Q&A, and a clear next step (sign up for a free 30-minute review that night).
Promotion: email, app notification, posters in branches, and partner with local employers.
Measure: attendance, review appointments booked, and new IRA and payroll-deduction accounts within 90 days.

Judge Q1: Start with the employer match, since it's an instant return, and open a Roth or traditional IRA. Catch-up contributions start at 50, so the next five years matter. Even $400 a month for 20 years at 7% grows to about $208,000, and delaying Social Security toward 70 raises guaranteed income.

Judge Q2: Be transparent and educational. Explain exactly how advisors are paid, give useful information members can act on even if they never book a meeting, and invite, don't pressure. As a not-for-profit credit union, the mission is the members, which is a message to lead with.
cases.title: RIVERBEND CREDIT UNION retirement seminar

cases.judge: CEO of a regional brokerage firm
cases.situation: The CEO (judge) of SUMMITPOINT INVESTMENTS wants to launch a low-cost robo-advisor app to attract younger investors, who currently use big online brokerages. The app would build and rebalance portfolios automatically and use AI chat to answer customer questions. The board is excited but worried about compliance, cybersecurity and protecting customer data.
tasks: Use of technology in financial-information management
Use of technology in compliance
Using CRM technology to serve investors
Use of technology in risk management
Legal considerations in the finance industry
questions: What if the AI chat gives a customer bad advice?
How do we compete with huge brokerages that already offer robo-advisors?
model: Open: 'Younger investors want low cost, simple and mobile. A robo-advisor can win them, if trust is built in from day one.'
Technology (FM:011): cloud platform with real-time data, automated portfolio building and rebalancing, ERP integration for accounting, encryption and firewalls.
Compliance technology (BL:149): automated KYC (ID plus selfie verification), sanctions screening, archiving every customer message, and suitability checks built into onboarding.
CRM (CR:024): track each customer's goals and life events, send personalized nudges (raise contributions after a raise), and measure customer lifetime value.
Risk technology (RM:042): intrusion detection, multifactor authentication, regular backups, and AI fraud monitoring. Test AI models for accuracy and bias, and keep humans reviewing.

Legal (BL:133): the firm is regulated by the SEC and FINRA; recommendations must meet Regulation Best Interest; provide Form CRS; customer accounts are protected by SIPC up to $500,000 if the firm fails (not against market losses).
Pricing: robo-advisors commonly charge around 0.25% a year or less; low cost is the main draw.
Visual: an onboarding flowchart from sign-up to first automated investment, with compliance checkpoints marked.

Judge Q1: Limit the AI to education and account help, not personal recommendations, with clear disclosures, and route anything about specific investment advice to a licensed human. Log every conversation for compliance, test the model regularly, and have a fast correction process. Regulators hold the firm responsible for what its tools say.

Judge Q2: Compete on what big firms can't easily match: local human advisors on call, personalized goal coaching through the CRM, and a lower minimum. Partner with local employers and credit unions to reach young workers, and make trust and transparency the brand.
cases.title: SUMMITPOINT's robo-advisor launch

cases.judge: president of a community bank being acquired
cases.situation: The president (judge) of MAPLE VALLEY BANK, a 70-year-old community bank, has agreed to be acquired by a larger regional bank. Account numbers, the mobile app and some fees will change in four months, and two of the bank's six branches will close. Longtime customers are already calling, worried about losing personal service. The president wants your team's plan for communicating the merger and keeping customers.
tasks: The nature of convergence and consolidation in banking
The role of financial institutions in the community
Interpreting new policies for customers
Handling customer complaints
Building trust during the transition
questions: Why should customers stay instead of moving to another local bank?
How should employees respond to a customer who is angry about the branch closing?
model: Open: 'Mergers succeed or fail on how customers feel. We'll make sure nobody is surprised.'

Consolidation (FI:573): the number of FDIC-insured institutions fell to 4,238 by mid-2026, from more than 17,000 in 1984. Mergers give scale: bigger ATM networks, better apps and more products. Recent examples include Capital One's 2025 acquisition of Discover.

Role of institutions (FI:336): the bank keeps deposits safe (FDIC insurance continues; during the transition, deposits at the two banks are insured separately for six months), lends locally and serves the community. Emphasize that local lending continues.
Interpret policies (CR:007): a plain-language guide: what changes, what doesn't, the dates, and what customers need to do (often nothing). Explain why each change happens and what's better.
Complaints (CR:010): Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank. Train every employee with answers to the top 10 questions and authority to waive a fee for upset customers.
Trust (EI:128): personal calls to the top 500 relationships, the same local bankers staying, a dedicated transition hotline, and branch 'welcome days' to learn the new app.
Timeline: letters and emails 90, 60 and 30 days out; app training sessions; extra staff in the first two weeks after conversion.
Measure: customer retention rate, complaint volume, app adoption and survey scores.

Judge Q1: Because the people they trust are staying, and now they'll have more: a larger ATM network, a better app and more loan options, with their deposits still FDIC-insured. We'll show exactly what improves for them and make the switch effortless.

Judge Q2: Listen without interrupting, acknowledge that the closing is a real inconvenience, and apologize for the disruption. Then solve: show the nearest branch and ATM, offer help setting up mobile deposit, and give a direct number for their banker. Thank them for being a customer and follow up in a week.
cases.title: MAPLE VALLEY BANK merger

cases.judge: owner of RIDGELINE CYCLES, a bike shop
cases.situation: RIDGELINE CYCLES has grown sales 30% in two years and the owner (judge) wants to open a second location. A bank has asked for financial statements and a clear explanation of how the expansion will be paid for. The owner is unsure whether to take a bank loan or bring in a partner who would invest money for a 30% ownership share.
tasks: Explain what the bank will look for in the business's financial statements
Compare debt financing (the loan) with equity financing (the partner)
Recommend a financing choice and explain how the owner should monitor the business after expanding
questions: What happens if sales at the new location are slower than expected?
Which single number should I watch most closely each month?
model: Open with the recommendation: a bank loan, if cash flow covers the payment with room to spare, so the owner keeps 100% control.
Need for financial info: the bank uses statements to judge capacity to repay and collateral (five Cs).
Balance sheet: show assets, liabilities, equity. The bank checks the current ratio and debt-to-equity.
Role of finance: obtain funds (debt vs equity), invest them (new location), manage working capital.
Debt: keep control, interest is tax-deductible, but a fixed payment is due even in slow months. Equity: no repayment, but you give up 30% of profits and decision-making forever.
Economic conditions: rising interest rates raise the loan's cost. A slowdown could hurt sales, so stress-test a 20% sales drop.
Plan: monthly cash flow review, keep 3 months of loan payments in reserve, keep the current ratio above 1.5, quarterly review with the banker.
Judge Q1: build a cash reserve now, start with a smaller lease, and keep a line of credit as backup.
Judge Q2: operating cash flow compared with the loan payment (debt service coverage).

cases.judge: CEO of SUMMIT CREDIT UNION
cases.situation: SUMMIT CREDIT UNION has 40,000 members. A regional insurance agency has offered to partner so Summit can sell auto and home insurance in its branches. The CEO (judge) wants to understand the trend of convergence and consolidation in financial services, how the partnership could affect members, and what risks to consider.
tasks: Explain convergence and consolidation in the financial industry
Describe how the partnership changes the role Summit plays for its members
Recommend whether to proceed and how to manage the risks
questions: How would we know in a year whether this was a good decision?
Why shouldn't we just merge with another credit union instead?
model: Recommend proceeding with a pilot partnership (bancassurance) in 2 branches for 12 months.
Role of financial institutions: Summit channels members' savings into loans. Insurance adds risk protection, so members get one-stop service.
Convergence = different sectors combining (credit union + insurance). Consolidation = same sector (merging with another credit union).
Financial markets: insurance market vs money and capital markets. Explain where each product fits.
Client responsibilities: suitability, no pressure selling, disclose that Summit earns commissions, protect member data.
ERM: list the risks in one integrated view. Reputational (bad insurer service), compliance (state insurance licensing), operational (staff training), strategic.
KPIs: share of members with 2+ products, member satisfaction score, complaint rate, commission revenue.

Judge Q1: set targets before the pilot starts: share of members with 2 or more products, member satisfaction above the current score, complaints per 1,000 policies, and commission revenue covering staff and training costs within 12 months.
Judge Q2: consolidation adds scale but doesn't add new products. Convergence meets more member needs.

cases.judge: owner of HARBOR HOME SERVICES, a plumbing company with 25 employees
cases.situation: HARBOR HOME SERVICES recently discovered that its office manager paid $38,000 over two years to a fake vendor she secretly set up. The office manager handled all invoices, payments and bank reconciliations alone. The owner (judge) wants to know how this happened and how to prevent it.
tasks: Explain why the fraud was possible
Recommend internal controls and technology to prevent and detect future fraud
Explain how risk management should work going forward
questions: We're a small company. Can we afford all of this?
How do I rebuild trust with my other employees?
model: Root cause: no separation of duties. One person approved, paid and reconciled.
Internal controls: split duties (one person enters invoices, the owner approves payments, an outside bookkeeper reconciles), dual signature over $2,500, an approved-vendor list.
Technology: accounting software with user permissions and audit trails. Data matching of employee addresses against vendor addresses. Bank alerts for new payees.
External controls: an annual external review by a CPA, and employee dishonesty (fidelity) insurance to transfer risk.
Ethics in risk management: a written code of conduct, a confidential reporting channel, and handling the case fairly and legally.
Risk process: identify, assess, control, monitor. Quarterly surprise reviews.
Judge Q1: most controls are free (process changes). Software costs about $50 to $100 a month, far less than the $38,000 loss.
Judge Q2: explain the controls protect everyone, keep things transparent, and avoid blame.

cases.judge: founder and CEO of PINECREST ORGANICS, a food company planning an IPO
cases.situation: PINECREST ORGANICS, a family-owned food company with $80 million in sales, plans to go public in two years. Right now the founder (judge) makes nearly every decision, the board is made up of three family members, and there is no internal audit function. Investment bankers say investors will demand stronger corporate governance.
tasks: Explain what corporate governance is and why investors care
Describe the components of a well-governed public company
Recommend a two-year plan to prepare Pinecrest's governance for the IPO
questions: Won't adding outside directors slow down my decisions?
What is the first thing I should do next month?
model: Governance = how a company is directed and controlled. Investors pay more for companies with accountability and transparency.
Components: an independent board (majority outside directors), audit committee, internal audit, external audit, code of conduct, transparent reporting, written bylaws.
Factors changing governance: going public brings SEC rules, Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control reporting and stock exchange listing standards.
Impact on decisions: the board approves strategy and major moves. The CEO still runs daily operations.
Compliance: build a compliance function, a record-retention policy and SOX-ready controls.

Plan: months 0-6 add 2 independent directors and write a code of conduct. Months 6-12 form an audit committee and hire an internal auditor. Months 12-24 do a SOX readiness test and quarterly reporting dry runs.
Judge Q1: some oversight slows decisions, but it lowers risk and raises the valuation investors will pay.
Judge Q2: recruit the first independent director with financial expertise to chair the audit committee.

cases.judge: CFO of LUMEN SPORTS, a sporting-goods retailer
cases.situation: Department managers at LUMEN SPORTS have gone over budget for three straight quarters. Budgets are set by the CFO (judge) at the start of the year and never change, even though sales swing a lot by season. Managers say the budgets are unrealistic. The CFO wants your recommendations.
tasks: Explain why the current budget process is failing
Describe how managerial accounting tools can improve budgeting and cost control
Recommend a new process and how to measure results
questions: How do I keep managers from padding their budgets?
How often should we review the numbers?
model: Root cause: a static, top-down budget doesn't flex with seasonal volume, and managers have no ownership.
Switch to a flexible budget: variable costs scale with sales, fixed costs stay fixed.
Variance analysis monthly: split price vs volume variances, and investigate only significant ones (management by exception).
Cost types: separate fixed vs variable and direct vs indirect. Judge managers only on costs they control.
Cost allocation: allocate shared costs like rent and IT by square feet or sales, and show them separately from controllable costs.
Budgeting software: what-if scenarios for peak and off-season.
Bottom-up budgeting with CFO review, so managers own their numbers.
KPIs: budget variance within ±5%, gross margin by department.
Judge Q1: compare to prior-year actuals and benchmarks, and reward accuracy, not just staying under budget.
Judge Q2: weekly sales and cash checks, a monthly variance review with each manager, a quarterly re-forecast for the rest of the year, and a full review at year end.

cases.judge: new client, a 34-year-old nurse who just inherited $60,000
cases.situation: A client (judge) just inherited $60,000 and has come to your advisory firm. She has $8,000 in credit card debt at 22% APR, no emergency fund, and contributes nothing to her employer's 401(k), which matches 4%. A coworker told her to put everything into a hot technology stock.
tasks: Explain your responsibilities to her as finance professionals
Explain how the time value of money and different investments apply to her situation
Recommend a plan for the $60,000
questions: Why shouldn't I just buy the stock my coworker recommended?
How will you keep my information private?
model: Duties: suitability, fiduciary care, disclose all fees and conflicts, confidentiality, understand her goals and risk tolerance first.
Step 1: pay off the 22% card. That's a guaranteed 22% 'return'.
Step 2: build a 6-month emergency fund (about $15,000) in a high-yield savings or money market account.
Step 3: contribute at least 4% to the 401(k) to capture the full match, which is free money.
Step 4: invest the rest in diversified, low-cost index funds, including some international exposure to avoid home bias.
TVM: $30,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to about $228,000 (FV = PV × 1.07^30, about 7.6×).
Herd mentality: one hot stock means concentration risk. Diversify instead.

Judge Q1: one stock is concentration risk. If that company stumbles, a big share of your inheritance goes with it. A coworker's tip isn't research, and following the crowd is herd mentality. A diversified index fund owns hundreds of companies, so no single one can sink you.
Judge Q2: privacy policy under Gramm-Leach-Bliley, encryption, and sharing nothing without her consent.

cases.judge: controller of CRESCENT LOGISTICS
cases.situation: CRESCENT LOGISTICS keeps customer, invoice and vendor records in separate spreadsheets maintained by different departments. Records are duplicated, numbers don't match across reports, and the controller (judge) spends days each month reconciling. An auditor also recommended testing the expense data for fraud.
tasks: Explain the role of financial-information management
Recommend how to organize the data and which tools to use
Explain how the company can use data analysis to detect fraud and improve decisions
questions: What's the biggest risk of moving everything to one system?
How will this help me make better decisions, not just faster reports?
model: FIM: collect, store, analyze and report accurate data so leaders can decide.
Normalize: one relational database or ERP with linked tables (customers, invoices, vendors) and unique keys, so each fact is stored once.
Queries and filters replace manual reconciliation.
Fraud tests: Benford's Law on expense amounts (measured data), and match employee addresses against vendor addresses.
Technology: automated data collection reduces entry errors. Cloud ERP brings cybersecurity risk, so use firewalls, multi-factor authentication, access permissions and backups.
Ethics: audit trails, confidentiality, record-retention schedule.
CRM link: customer data in one hub reveals profitable customers.
Judge Q1: a data migration error or security breach. Reduce it by testing, running old and new systems in parallel for a month, and training staff.

Judge Q2: one clean database lets you build dashboards that compare actual results to budget in real time, rank customers by profitability, and test what-if scenarios, so decisions rest on current numbers instead of last month's spreadsheets.

cases.judge: managing director of ATLAS WEALTH PARTNERS, an investment firm
cases.situation: A junior broker at ATLAS WEALTH PARTNERS was caught buying shares for his own account minutes before executing large client orders in the same stock. A second advisor has been heavily promoting a small, unknown stock in online forums. The managing director (judge) wants to understand the legal exposure and build a stronger compliance program.
tasks: Identify the illegal or unethical practices involved
Explain legal considerations and the role of compliance in finance
Recommend a compliance program, including technology
questions: What should I tell our clients?
How do we make sure this never happens again?
model: Practice 1 = front-running (illegal). Practice 2 may be a pump and dump, depending on whether he owns and sells the stock.
Legal: SEC and FINRA rules, Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Possible fines, bans and lawsuits.
Compliance: prevent, detect, correct. Chief compliance officer, written policies, annual training.
Technology: trade surveillance software flags employee trades near client orders, and social media monitoring.
Ethics in finance: trust is the product. Violations hurt clients and markets.
Governance: board-level compliance reporting, code of conduct, whistleblower hotline.
Judge Q1: be transparent, explain the corrective actions, and compensate any harmed clients.

Judge Q2: a clear written policy (no personal trades near client orders, pre-clearance for employee trades), trade-surveillance software, annual training with sign-off, a whistleblower hotline, and real consequences that are applied consistently.

cases.judge: owner of BRIGHTSIDE DOG GROOMING, open one year
cases.situation: BRIGHTSIDE DOG GROOMING made a profit in its first year according to its income statement, yet the owner (judge) often struggles to pay suppliers on time and nearly missed payroll twice. Many customers are businesses (kennels) that pay 60 days after service. The owner wants to understand what's going on.
tasks: Explain how the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement each tell part of the story
Explain why a profitable business can run short of cash
Recommend actions to improve cash flow
questions: Should I just get a bigger loan?
How often should I look at each statement?
model: Income statement = profit over a period, using accrual revenue (earned, not yet collected).
Balance sheet: large accounts receivable mean cash is tied up in unpaid kennel invoices.
Cash flow statement: operating cash flow is low even though net income is positive.
Need for info: the statements show the gap. Track AR days (365 ÷ AR turnover).
Role of finance: working capital management.
Actions: shorten terms to 30 days, offer a 2% discount for paying in 10 days, require deposits, send invoices immediately, add a small line of credit for gaps.
Judge Q1: a loan treats the symptom. Fix collections first, then use a line of credit as a safety net.
Judge Q2: cash weekly, income statement and cash flow monthly, balance sheet monthly or quarterly.

cases.judge: investment committee chair of NORTHWIND COMMUNITY FOUNDATION
cases.situation: NORTHWIND COMMUNITY FOUNDATION has a $5 million endowment invested 100% in U.S. large-company stocks. Interest rates and inflation have been volatile, and the committee chair (judge) is worried about a recession. Some board members want to add international and emerging-market investments; others think that's too risky.
tasks: Explain how economic conditions affect financial markets
Explain financial globalization and the case for international diversification
Recommend an allocation approach and how to read the information needed to monitor it
questions: Isn't investing overseas just gambling?
What reports should our committee review each quarter?
model: Economy and markets: in contractions stocks fall. Rising rates lower bond prices. Defensive sectors hold up better.
Home bias: 100% domestic concentration ignores diversification benefits.
Globalization: international markets don't move in lockstep with the US, so they can lower overall volatility. Emerging markets add growth but more instability and currency risk.
Recommend: diversified mix, for example 50% US stocks, 15% developed international, 5% emerging, 25% bonds, 5% cash, rebalanced yearly. Not personal advice; set by an investment policy statement.
Monitoring sources: fund annual reports, 10-K and 10-Q filings, stock tables (52-week range, yield, P/E), relative strength.
ERM: the board's risk appetite, documented in an investment policy statement.
Judge Q1: it isn't gambling. Diversification reduces risk, and the position is a modest, measured slice.

Judge Q2: performance versus a benchmark, the asset mix versus the investment policy statement's targets, fees and expenses, the largest holdings and any concentration, and a short note on market and economic conditions.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) says: "I can afford a $40,000 truck, so why shouldn't I buy it?" Explain the real cost.
drills.model: Being able to afford it isn't the whole story; the real cost is the opportunity cost. Say a used truck would do the same job for $25,000. The extra $15,000 could go into a Roth IRA instead, and at a 7% average return it could grow to roughly $58,000 in 20 years. Interest is a price too: a bigger loan at today's rates means paying more for the same years of driving. So our advice is to pick the truck that meets your needs, then put the difference to work.

drills.scenario: A first-time buyer (judge) asks: "Rates are about 7%. Why haven't home prices dropped?"
drills.model: It's supply and demand. Higher rates did cool demand, but they cut supply even more: millions of owners have mortgages below 4% and don't want to sell and give that up. Fewer homes for sale means buyers still compete, so prices stay high. With the 30-year rate near 7.11% in November 2026, the smart move is to buy only when the payment fits, about 28% of gross income, and plan to refinance if rates fall. Waiting for prices to crash could take years.

drills.scenario: A judge asks your team to explain GDP in plain language and say what last quarter's number means for a small business.
drills.model: GDP is the total value of everything the country produces in a period, from haircuts to cars. Real GDP removes inflation so we can see if we actually made more. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, which means the economy is expanding: more spending, more hiring. For a small business, that's a decent time to grow, but GDP looks backward, so we'd still keep a cash reserve and a line of credit in case growth slows.

drills.scenario: A recent graduate (judge) asks: "Unemployment is only about 4%, so why can't my cousin find a job?"
drills.model: A low overall rate doesn't mean every job seeker finds work quickly. Some unemployment is frictional, people between jobs; some is structural, when skills don't match the jobs open, like tellers replaced by apps. Your cousin may be in a field with fewer openings. The fix is human capital: a short certificate in a growing field or new skills that match job postings. Meanwhile, a part-time job keeps income coming and builds experience.

drills.scenario: A coffee shop owner (judge) says costs are up 8% this year and asks whether to raise prices.
drills.model: Yes, but selectively. With inflation at 3.7% and your costs up 8%, absorbing it all would shrink your margin. Raise prices most on drinks customers love and can't easily find elsewhere, like specialty lattes, and hold prices on basics that customers compare. Small, regular increases cause less pushback than one big jump. Cut waste and renegotiate with your milk supplier too. That protects profit without sending loyal customers to the chain down the street.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks: "The Fed raised rates again. What does that mean for me?"
drills.model: It depends which side of the rate you're on. The Fed raised its target to 3.75%-4.00% in September 2026 to slow inflation. As a saver, you win: high-yield savings and CDs pay more. As a borrower, you lose, especially on variable debt: credit cards and home equity lines move with the prime rate, now about 7%. So we'd pay down your credit card first, move savings to a high-yield account, and lock a fixed rate on any new loan.

drills.scenario: A salon owner (judge) asks how to prepare for a recession that might or might not come.
drills.model: Prepare while times are good, because that's when banks lend easily. First, build cash reserves of three to six months of fixed costs. Second, open a line of credit now, even if you don't use it. Third, keep some costs flexible, like booth rentals or part-time staff. Salons are discretionary, so clients stretch visits in a downturn, but loyalty programs and memberships keep them coming. The 2020 recession lasted two months and 2008's lasted 18; reserves get you through either.

drills.scenario: A gift shop owner (judge) asks: "Who actually pays for tariffs?"
drills.model: The importer pays the tariff first: when your goods arrive, you or your supplier pay the tax at the border. Then the cost gets shared. You can raise prices, which shifts some to customers; accept a lower margin; or switch to a supplier in a lower-tariff country. The average effective U.S. tariff rate was about 6.7% in July 2026, but around 23% on goods from China. So we'd check where each product comes from and price the most affected items accordingly.

drills.scenario: An exporter (judge) asks: "Is a strong dollar good or bad for my business?"
drills.model: For an exporter, a strong dollar is mostly a headwind. It makes your products more expensive for foreign buyers, and payments in yen or euros convert into fewer dollars. In November 2026 a dollar bought about 159 yen, near a multi-year high. It does help on the cost side if you import materials. To manage it, we'd use forward contracts to lock exchange rates on confirmed orders and price in a way that keeps you competitive.

drills.scenario: A judge asks: "How does a bank make money, and how is that different from an app like Chime?"
drills.model: A traditional bank mainly earns the spread: it pays depositors one rate and lends that money out at a higher rate, plus fees. A fintech like Chime earns mostly interchange fees, the small cut merchants pay each time a member swipes a debit card, according to its 2025 IPO filing. That's why fintechs push card use and banks push loans. For a bank competing with Chime, the edge is lending and advice, so we'd lead with fast personal and small-business loans.

drills.scenario: A judge playing a client says: "Our overseas agent wants a small payment to an official to speed up our permit. It's normal there. Okay?"
drills.model: No, and here's why. The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act makes paying a foreign official to win or speed up business a federal crime for U.S. companies, even overseas. Penalties can reach billions: Siemens paid about $1.6 billion in 2008. Beyond the law, it signals that your company can be pressured again. Decline politely, document the request, report it to legal, and use a licensed customs broker and official channels. A slower permit is far cheaper than a bribery case.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) is meeting investors from Japan next week and asks how to prepare.
drills.model: Research the business culture and focus on relationships first. Japan is a high-context culture: meaning comes from relationships and tone, not just words. Exchange business cards with both hands and read them before putting them away. Expect decisions to take time, because they're often made by group consensus, so don't push for an answer in the first meeting. Bring materials in Japanese if possible and confirm next steps in writing afterward. Respect builds the trust that closes deals.

drills.scenario: A bakery owner (judge) asks: "Sales are up. Should I hire two more bakers?"
drills.model: Maybe not, because of diminishing returns. With one oven, each extra baker adds less output: if the third baker added 50 loaves but a fourth would add only 20, the oven is your bottleneck. Two more bakers would mostly wait their turn while costing full wages. Instead, we'd finance a second oven, which raises every baker's productivity. Compare the extra output to the cost: equipment that doubles capacity usually beats paying for people who can't use it.

drills.scenario: A town council member (judge) asks: "Why should our town care whether small businesses survive?"
drills.model: Because small businesses are the local economy. Nationally, they're 99.9% of all businesses and employ about 46% of workers, according to the SBA. Locally, they hire neighbors, buy from local suppliers and pay taxes that fund schools and roads, and the money they earn gets spent again in town. They also keep big chains competitive. So the town can help with a small-business loan fund through local banks and simple permitting, which pays back in jobs and tax revenue.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) says: "I keep my money in savings because the stock market is basically gambling. Why should I invest?"
drills.model: Saving and investing do different jobs. Savings is for safety and emergencies, and you should keep three to six months there. But money that sits at a low rate loses buying power to inflation every year. Investing in a diversified index fund isn't betting on one company; you own a slice of hundreds of businesses. Since 1928 the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 10% a year, with bad years along the way, so it's for money you won't need for at least five years. Gambling has a negative expected return; owning businesses has historically had a positive one.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) says: "I always mean to invest, but at the end of the month there's nothing left." Recommend a fix.
drills.model: The fix is to stop relying on willpower and automate it. Pay yourself first: set up an automatic transfer the day after payday. Brokerages like Fidelity, Schwab and Vanguard let you schedule recurring investments into an S&P 500 index fund for as little as a few dollars, and many offer fractional shares. Start with an amount you won't miss, like 5% of take-home pay, and raise it 1% every time you get a raise. Dollar-cost averaging means you buy more shares when prices dip. In a year you'll have invested without ever deciding to.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks: "How do I know you're working for me and not for your company?"
drills.model: That's exactly the right question. First, we'll tell you in writing how we're paid, whether that's a flat fee, a percentage of assets or commissions, so you can see any conflicts. Second, we're held to a best-interest standard: our recommendations must fit your goals, risk tolerance and time horizon, and we document why. Third, you can verify us yourself: look us up on FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's adviser search to see licenses and any complaints. And you'll always get our recommendation and the reasons, so the decision stays yours.

drills.scenario: A new parent (judge) asks: "Should I buy term or whole life insurance?"
drills.model: For most young families, term life is the better fit. It covers you for a set period, like 20 or 30 years, which matches the years your child depends on you, and it costs a fraction of whole life for the same coverage. A common rule of thumb is coverage of 10 to 12 times your income. Whole life lasts forever and builds cash value, but premiums can be many times higher. Many planners suggest buying term and investing the difference in a retirement account. We'd also add disability insurance, since you're more likely to miss work from injury than to die young.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks: "If my bank or brokerage goes under, do I lose everything?"
drills.model: No, there are two safety nets. At a bank, the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and credit unions get the same through the NCUA. In 2023, when Silicon Valley Bank failed, insured depositors kept every dollar. At a brokerage, SIPC protects up to $500,000, including $250,000 in cash, if the firm itself fails. What SIPC doesn't do is protect you from the market going down. So the plan is: keep deposits under the limits at each bank and spread large balances across institutions.

drills.scenario: A 19-year-old with a part-time job (judge) asks: "Roth IRA or traditional IRA?"
drills.model: At 19, the Roth is usually the winner. You pay tax on the money now, while your tax rate is low, and then every dollar of growth comes out tax-free in retirement. The limit is $7,500 for 2026 and 2027, but you can only contribute up to what you earned. A traditional IRA gives you a deduction now, which matters more when you're in a higher bracket. Bonus: Roth contributions, not earnings, can come out any time, so it doubles as flexible savings. Even $50 a month at 19 could grow to well over $150,000 by retirement.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks: "How can I raise my credit score fast? I want to buy a car in six months."
drills.model: There are two levers that move fastest. First is utilization, which is about 30% of your FICO score: pay balances down so you use under 30% of your limits, and under 10% is even better. Second is payment history, the biggest factor at about 35%: put every bill on autopay so nothing is ever late. Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute any errors. Don't open or close cards right before applying. In six months, those steps can make a real difference, and that can save you hundreds on the loan.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) has four credit cards and asks which to pay off first.
drills.model: Make the minimum on every card so nothing goes late, then throw every extra dollar at one card at a time. The math says go highest interest rate first; that's the avalanche method and it saves the most money. If motivation is the problem, the snowball method pays off the smallest balance first for a quick win. Either works if you stick with it. Also call each card company and ask for a lower rate, since many will say yes. And once a card is paid off, keep it open with a small autopaid bill to protect your score.

drills.scenario: A grandparent (judge) wants to help pay for a newborn grandchild's college. What do you recommend?
drills.model: A 529 plan is the strongest tool. The money grows tax-free when it's used for qualified education costs, and many states give a state tax deduction. Starting at birth gives 18 years of compounding: $100 a month at 6% grows to almost $39,000. If the child gets a scholarship or skips college, you can change the beneficiary to another family member, and under SECURE 2.0 up to $35,000 can roll into the child's Roth IRA. For 2026, you can give up to $19,000 a year per person without filing a gift tax return.

drills.scenario: A nervous client (judge) says: "Everyone says a recession is coming. Should I sell everything?"
drills.model: I understand the worry, but selling everything usually turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss. Nobody times the market consistently, and some of the best days often come right after the worst. The S&P 500 fell about 37% in 2008 and fully recovered within a few years for people who stayed invested. What we can control is your plan: keep an emergency fund so you never have to sell in a downturn, make sure your stock and bond mix matches your timeline, and keep investing monthly so you buy at lower prices. Following the herd is how people buy high and sell low.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) starting a dog-grooming business asks whether to be a sole proprietor or an LLC.
drills.model: A sole proprietorship is the simplest: no filing in most states and you keep all the profit, but you're personally liable, so if a dog is injured and you're sued, your house and savings are at risk. An LLC costs a small state filing fee but separates your personal assets from business debts and lawsuits, and profits still pass through to your personal tax return. Since grooming involves animals and customer property, I'd recommend an LLC plus general liability insurance. Open a separate business bank account so the protection holds up.

drills.scenario: A coffee cart owner (judge) has $4,000 in monthly fixed costs. Each drink sells for $5 and costs $1.80 to make. How many drinks to break even, and what does it mean?
drills.model: Each drink contributes $5 minus $1.80, which is $3.20, toward fixed costs. $4,000 divided by $3.20 is 1,250 drinks a month, about 57 a day over 22 working days. Below that you lose money; every drink above it is profit. To lower the break-even, you can raise prices slightly, cut the cost per drink with bulk buying, or reduce fixed costs like rent. I'd track daily sales against that 57-drink target every day.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks: "Why does inflation matter for my savings?"
drills.model: Inflation is a hidden tax on cash. If prices rise 3.7% a year, as they did in the year through September 2026, $10,000 in an account paying 0.25% buys about $345 less a year later. Over ten years at 3% inflation, money sitting still loses about a quarter of its buying power. That's why you keep only emergency money in basic savings, use high-yield savings or CDs paying around 4% for short-term goals, and invest long-term money in assets like stocks that historically beat inflation.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) received a text saying their bank account is locked and to click a link. What do you tell them?
drills.model: Don't click it. That's a phishing scam, and texts like this are one of the most common ways criminals steal logins. Real banks won't ask you to verify your account through a link or ask for a one-time passcode. Instead, open the bank's app directly or call the number on the back of your card. To protect yourself going forward, turn on multifactor authentication with an authenticator app, set alerts for every transaction, and freeze your credit with all three bureaus for free. If you did click, change your password immediately and call the bank.

drills.scenario: The judge, a bank HR director, asks your team: "What finance careers fit someone who loves helping people and is good with numbers?"
drills.model: Personal financial planning is a great match: you help families with budgets, investing, insurance and retirement, and the CFP certification is the gold standard. Other options are credit counselor, loan officer, private banker and insurance agent. If you like numbers more than client work, look at financial analyst or accountant, with the CPA. To get started: join DECA and FBLA, take an internship or volunteer with a free tax-prep program, and network through informational interviews. Building relationships early matters because most advisors grow through referrals.

drills.scenario: You are an accounting associate at a sporting-goods retailer whose department managers keep going over budget. The CFO (judge) wants your recommendations.
drills.model: The root problem is a fixed budget that ignores seasonal swings, and managers who don't own their numbers. First, variance analysis: each month compare budget to actual, split into price and volume, and dig into only the big gaps. Second, switch to a flexible budget that scales variable costs with sales, built bottom-up with each manager. We'd target variances within 5%, starting next quarter.

drills.scenario: You are a financial advisor. A young client (judge) wants to open her first checking account and asks whether to choose a bank or a credit union.
drills.model: Both are safe if insured: FDIC for banks, NCUA for credit unions, up to $250,000. A credit union is member-owned and not-for-profit, so it usually has lower fees and better loan rates. A big bank may offer more branches and better apps. My job is to match your needs, so for low fees and a future car loan I'd start with a credit union. Let's compare monthly fees and ATM access before you open it.

drills.scenario: You are an analyst. Your bank's president (judge) asks what 'convergence' means and whether the bank should start selling insurance.
drills.model: Convergence is when firms from different financial sectors combine, like banks and insurers. Consolidation is same-sector mergers. Selling insurance through our branches, called bancassurance, adds fee income and one-stop service for customers already in the insurance market. I'd pilot it in a few branches with a licensed partner, train staff on suitability, and track products per customer and complaints for 12 months.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) asks why she should start investing $2,000 now instead of waiting ten years.
drills.model: It's the time value of money: a dollar today can earn returns that compound. At 7%, $2,000 grows to about $3,934 in 10 years and about $7,740 in 20. Wait ten years and you lose that whole first decade of compounding. Start now with a low-cost index fund, add a set amount every month, and we'll review it each year.

drills.scenario: You are a risk analyst. The CEO (judge) asks how enterprise risk management differs from what the company does now: each department handles its own risks.
drills.model: Right now risks sit in silos, so no one sees how a cyberattack, a key supplier failure and a recession could hit at once. ERM pulls every risk into one risk inventory, rated by likelihood and impact, with an owner for each. Internal controls handle what we can control. Insurance and contingency plans cover external risks like inflation. I'd start a quarterly risk committee reporting to the board.

drills.scenario: You are a consultant. A startup founder (judge) asks why investors keep asking about 'corporate governance.'
drills.model: Governance is how a company is directed and controlled, and investors see it as protection for their money. Strong governance means an independent board, an audit committee, internal and external audits, a code of conduct and transparent reporting. That lowers the risk of fraud and mismanagement, which raises the valuation. Your first step: add one independent director with finance experience in the next 90 days.

drills.scenario: You are a compliance officer. Your managing director (judge) asks why a broker buying a stock right before a client's big order is a problem.
drills.model: That's front-running. It's illegal because the broker profits from confidential client information at the client's expense. It breaks fiduciary duty and SEC/FINRA rules, and it can bring fines, bans and lost trust. Compliance should prevent, detect and correct: trade surveillance software that flags employee trades near client orders, pre-clearance of personal trades, and annual training.

drills.scenario: You are a client-services manager at an investment firm. The firm's president (judge) asks whether CRM software is worth the cost.
drills.model: Yes. CRM puts every client's data and interactions in one hub, so advisors give consistent, personal service. It reveals sales opportunities, like a client who just bought a home and needs insurance, and flags clients at risk of leaving. People still have to judge which data matters and protect client confidentiality. We'd track client retention and products per client after six months.

drills.scenario: You are an internal auditor. The controller (judge) asks how to check expense reports for fraud without reviewing all 40,000.
drills.model: Use data analysis instead of reading everything. Benford's Law says that in real, measured amounts, the leading digit 1 shows up about 30% of the time. Made-up numbers usually break that pattern, so we test the data and flag outliers. Then we filter by employee and by just-under-approval-limit amounts, and match employee addresses against vendor addresses. We review only the flagged items, which saves weeks.

drills.scenario: A new bakery owner (judge) asks why she needs three different financial statements.
drills.model: Each statement answers a different question. The income statement shows whether you made a profit over a period: sales minus costs. The balance sheet shows what you own and owe on one date. The cash flow statement shows whether cash is actually coming in, because you can be profitable and still run out of cash. Review cash weekly and the full set monthly so you catch problems early.

drills.scenario: A manager (judge) wants to keep funding a failing project because 'we've already spent $200,000 on it.'
drills.model: That $200,000 is a sunk cost. It's gone whatever we decide, so it shouldn't drive the decision. Use marginal analysis: compare the additional cost to finish with the additional benefit we expect. If the next $80,000 brings in less than $80,000 in value, stop and redirect the money to the best alternative, which is the opportunity cost.

drills.scenario: A student intern (judge) asks your advice on how to build a network in the finance industry.
drills.model: Start with professional associations: join a student chapter of a group like the CFA Society or a local finance association, and volunteer for a committee. Go to conferences and seminars and follow up within 48 hours. Ask for informational interviews. And keep in touch with contacts by sharing useful articles. Set a goal of three new professional contacts a month.

drills.scenario: You are an IT-finance analyst. The CFO (judge) asks whether moving the accounting system to the cloud is a good idea.
drills.model: Cloud accounting gives anywhere access, automatic updates and automated data collection that cuts entry errors. The main risk is a cybersecurity breach, so require multi-factor authentication, encryption, role-based access and a vendor with strong security audits. Keep off-site backups. I'd pilot it for one quarter alongside the current system before switching fully.

drills.scenario: An investor (judge) asks what the statement of changes in equity tells her that the other statements don't.
drills.model: It shows exactly why the owners' stake changed during the period: starting equity, plus net income and new stock issued, minus dividends and buybacks, equals ending equity. That tells you how much profit the company kept to reinvest versus paid out. You'll find it in the annual report and the 10-K. Read it alongside the income statement each year.

drills.scenario: A client (judge) sold stocks this year with $9,000 in gains and wants to know how to reduce the tax.
drills.model: Capital losses offset capital gains, so selling losing positions this year (tax-loss harvesting) could cut the taxable gain. Gains on assets held over one year get lower long-term rates than short-term gains. Charitable donations of appreciated stock can also help. I'm not your CPA, so we'd confirm with your tax preparer before December 31.
